If the endpoint has no per-request nonce/timestamp binding and the session cookie is not re-validated, it still succeeds = persistent hidden backdoor.
techniques.payload: capture PUT /authentication/password (or /account/email) in Repeater -> logout (confirm replay now fails) -> log in fresh in another browser -> replay the ORIGINAL captured request unchanged -> did it succeed?
techniques.tell: the logout-then-relogin step is what makes it a finding rather than a normal repeat. Fits our console/Repeater SOP exactly. Test on EVERY security-critical write. Contrast with a correctly-built endpoint: rotating CSRF/nonce or old-password re-check should break the replay.

techniques.technique: PRIVATE FIELD LEAKED THROUGH A SHARED/GROUP OBJECT: joining a shared container (leaderboard, org, project, team, workspace, shared album) makes members' PRIVATE fields (email, phone, real name) visible to other members / the creator, ignoring the user's own privacy setting.
techniques.payload: create the shared object -> invite the victim account -> after they accept, read the members/participants endpoint (and its raw JSON, not just the UI) -> compare against the victim's privacy settings
techniques.tell: the API response usually carries MORE fields than the UI renders - always read the raw JSON. Low barrier + harvestable at scale = accepted privacy finding. Directly applicable to any org/project/team member listing (SaaS multi-tenant).

techniques.technique: PARAM-VALIDATION-BEFORE-AUTHZ MASKS AN UNTESTED ENDPOINT: a 400 'required query parameter X not set' is NOT a denial - the authz check never ran. Naive testing records it as ENFORCED and moves on, leaving the endpoint genuinely untested.
techniques.payload: re-issue with every required param filled from your OWN working request (copy the exact param set the app sends), THEN judge; keep an own-object control in the same batch to prove the param set is right
techniques.tell: dogfooded: a cloud control-plane's credential endpoint 400'd on a missing db/role param for BOTH the foreign and own object; only after supplying them did the foreign call return a real 404-deny. Treat 400/422 shape-errors as UNTESTED, never as ENFORCED.

techniques.technique: PROGRAM-PUBLISHED ARTEFACTS CAN BE AN AUDIT MAP: some programs attach an endpoint inventory to the policy. If it carries a status column (e.g. 'IDOR: Found, remediated' / 'to be remediated'), it partitions the surface for you: already-audited = dupe risk, blank-with-identifier = never checked = hunt there.
techniques.payload: parse the attachment; split rows into audited vs unaudited-with-identifier; also DIFF it against endpoints seen in your own capture - endpoints present in traffic but ABSENT from the sheet are both unaudited AND undocumented (best odds)
techniques.tell: on a serverless-DB program the sheet held 156 endpoints: 28 audited, 87 unaudited-with-identifier; the live capture exposed several more (branch credentials, buckets, auth/users) that were not in the sheet at all. Read every policy attachment before testing.

techniques.technique: PERMISSIVE CORS != IMPACT when cookies are SameSite=Lax/Strict. A credentialed cross-origin fetch can resolve 200 (server reflects arbitrary Origin + Allow-Credentials) yet return an EMPTY/anonymous body because the browser never attached the session cookie.
techniques.payload: PROOF SEQUENCE: (1) log in at the target origin, (2) confirm the authed endpoint returns real data THERE, (3) check the session cookie's SameSite/HttpOnly in Application->Cookies, (4) re-request from an unrelated origin (example.com) with credentials:'include' - only DATA returned there is a finding
techniques.tell: reflected-Origin + Allow-Credentials looks like a classic CORS bug and gets mass-reported; without SameSite=None (or a Bearer/token path the attacker can reach) there is NO cross-site read = non-qualifying. Escalate only if the app sets SameSite=None or accepts the token via a header an attacker can supply.

techniques.technique: SPA BUNDLE MINING v2 — when literal '/api/vN/...' strings are rare, the app builds paths from TEMPLATE LITERALS with an axios baseURL. Mine for RESOURCE-WORD fragments instead, normalise ${...}->{id}, then filter out CSS-module classes (_name_hash_12), analytics event ids (*_clicked/_cta/_error) and asset paths.
techniques.payload: 1) grab the vite chunk manifest from the entry bundle (__vite__mapDeps  m.f=[...]) -> gives EVERY lazy chunk name; 2) download all chunks from the CDN with xargs (curl in a while-read loop silently eats stdin and downloads nothing); 3) regex resource words (projects|organizations|branches|api_keys|billing|users/me|auth|subscriptions...) inside quotes/backticks
techniques.tell: dogfooded on a serverless-DB console: naive /api/v2 regex found 42, the manifest+fragment method found 104 tenant paths + 36 internal /admin/* staff routes. In-page fetch of the bundle can be blocked by CSP connect-src even though script-src allows it — list URLs in the browser, download them out-of-band.

techniques.technique: REMOVE THE MEMBERSHIP, THEN RE-RUN. The cleanest way to settle an ambiguous cross-tenant 200 is to strip the tester's membership/collaborator role from the victim tenant and repeat the exact request. Member-legitimate access flips to a denial; a real authz bug keeps returning data.
techniques.payload: as victim-admin: remove the attacker account from the org/team -> as attacker: re-issue the SAME request + a 'GET /users/me/memberships' identity check in the same batch (the membership list must no longer contain the victim org)
techniques.tell: dogfooded 3x in one session (a legit 'developer' member, a shared folder, and a usage-history endpoint). Test accounts accumulate memberships during a hunt and quietly turn later BOLA tests into self-access. Cheapest possible discriminator - one UI click plus one re-run.

techniques.technique: URL-FETCHER GUARD CHARACTERISATION: when a feature legitimately fetches a user-supplied URL (JWKS/webhook/avatar/import), an OOB callback proves NOTHING by itself - that is the feature. Map the guard by DIFFERENTIAL ERROR MESSAGES before claiming SSRF.
techniques.payload: probe set: http:// vs https:// | literal private IP (127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254, 10.x) | userinfo confusion https://good.host@1.2.3.4/ | query string present/absent | explicit :port | file://,gopher:// | PUBLIC HOSTNAME RESOLVING TO PRIVATE IP (localtest.me -> 127.0.0.1, <ip>.nip.io) | 30x redirect from an allowed host
techniques.tell: distinct messages map the layers: 'must use HTTPS' = scheme allowlist; 'invalid URL' = pre-fetch string/parser validation; 'error fetching' = validation PASSED and a connection was attempted (no DNS-resolution guard); parse error like 'invalid JWKS' = it CONNECTED and read a body. That last pair is a connected-vs-not ORACLE. ⚠️ HTTPS-only kills cloud metadata (IMDS is HTTP-only). Blind + no content reflection + needing internal port-scanning to show impact = NOT reportable under most policies, and scanning breaks no-automated-scanning RoE.

techniques.technique: GRAPHQL GLOBAL-ID ENUMERATION, VERDICT ON SIDE-EFFECT NOT RESPONSE: Relay-style ids are base64 of `gid://<app>/<Type>/<int>` - decode, increment the int, re-encode. The killer nuance: the mutation may answer with an ERROR while still performing the action. On H1's own AddTagToAssets the response was `{"errors":[{"message":"AsmTag does not exist","type":"NOT_FOUND"}]}` yet the victim's private tag was disclosed on the attacker's assets page.
techniques.payload: atob(tagId) -> gid://hackerone/AsmTag/4979xxxx ; btoa('gid://<app>/<Type>/<n±1>') ; replay mutation ; THEN RELOAD THE UI/LIST ENDPOINT and diff
techniques.tell: An error body is NOT a denial. After every rejected-looking mutation, re-read the object list through a second channel (UI page, list query, export) and diff against a pre-state snapshot. Sequential integer ids inside base64 = enumeration is trivial; the base64 is obfuscation, not authz.

techniques.technique: SUPPORT/LIVE-CHAT WIDGETS AS THE NON-SPA SINK: the main app is React (auto-escaped) but the bolted-on support chat, ticket system, or agent console is often a different stack that renders raw HTML - and the audience is STAFF, which converts plain HTML injection into employee phishing.
techniques.payload: CLICK ; ; fake UI text mimicking internal instructions
techniques.tell: Sinks the SPA sweep misses: chat transcripts, ticket bodies, agent-side admin views, notification emails, PDF/CSV exports. ⚠️ Many programs list HTML-injection as a KNOWN no-award (Neon did) - check the savers list FIRST; it only pays where the render is agent-facing (phishing) or lands in an href.

techniques.technique: STATE-CHANGING GET = CSRF WITH NO TOKEN NEEDED: settings toggles implemented as GET (`/account/network?usingAltSocket=false`) are exploitable by a bare or - anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite=Lax, and CORS are all irrelevant because it is a top-level navigation.
techniques.payload: click ;
techniques.tell: Grep the route table for GET handlers that mutate: /enable, /disable, /toggle, /set, /switch, /opt-in, ?flag=, ?mode=. SameSite=Lax still SENDS cookies on top-level GET navigation - that is the whole point. Low severity alone; pairs upward if the toggle disables a security control (2FA, session pinning, routing).

techniques.technique: LOCKOUT KEYED ON USERNAME = ATTACKER-CONTROLLED ACCOUNT DoS: if failed-login throttling counts per-ACCOUNT instead of per-IP/session/fingerprint, anyone who knows a username can lock any user out on demand.
techniques.payload: 5-10 failed logins vs a known username, then PROVE the victim is locked by logging in with the CORRECT password from a DIFFERENT IP
techniques.tell: The proof step is what makes it reportable - correct creds + clean IP + still throttled = the lock is bound to the identity, not the attacker. Feed usernames from public directories/leaderboards. ⚠️ Check scope first: many programs list rate-limiting and DoS as OUT OF SCOPE, and generating lockouts against real users is off-limits - use your own second account as the victim.

techniques.technique: RAW CLIENT IP IN OUTBOUND EMAIL (login alerts, security notices): the address traverses SMTP relays, spam filters, logs and backups in cleartext at each hop, and under GDPR an IP is PII - argued as data-minimisation failure (CWE-200/359) rather than a technical flaw.
techniques.payload: trigger a login-alert / new-device / password-reset email and read the raw body for a literal client IP or reverse-DNS hostname
techniques.tell: LOW-VALUE CLASS - expect Informative/N-A on most programs, and it is pure policy argument with no exploit chain. Only worth writing where the program explicitly rewards privacy/GDPR issues. Recommend approximate city/country or an in-dashboard activity log instead.

techniques.technique: DECODE THE APP'S OWN SESSION COOKIE BEFORE DEBUGGING A GENERIC 400: bot-managed sites answer a flagged session with a generic validation error, sending you hunting for input bugs that do not exist. The verdict is usually sitting in a base64 cookie the app set itself.
techniques.payload: base64url-decode every cookie that looks structured (one target: a __Secure-* session cookie -> {"s":["ANONYMOUS","BOT","BOT_SUSPECTED"]}) ; then fingerprint the vendor from headers/cookies: Kasada = X-Kpsdk-Ct/-Cd/-H/-V + KP_UIDz + a multi-KB `session` blob in the body | Akamai = _abck/bm_sz | PerimeterX = _px/_pxhd | DataDome = datadome | Cloudflare = cf_clearance/__cf_bm
techniques.tell: Flagged BEFORE any submit = the wall, not your payload. Tells it apart from a real geo-block: a geo-block names the country and the request usually carries a country field - that target's register body had NO country and wn_consent said region_type:UNRESTRICTED. ⚠️ Do NOT attempt to defeat a bot manager: out of bounds for us and breaches most policies. Screen the vendor with ONE page load before spending time on a target; consumer-retail/marketplace + Kasada/Akamai/PerimeterX has now killed 3 targets from the same IP.

techniques.technique: PAYWALL BYPASS BY POSTING THE SETTING DIRECTLY: premium-only toggles are frequently gated in the UI only - the settings endpoint accepts the field from any authenticated user with no entitlement check. On pixiv a free account disabled ads by POSTing {"setting":{"showAds":false}} to /_api/update_user_setting.
techniques.payload: POST /api/.../user_setting|preferences|profile with the premium field set ; also try PATCH/PUT ; flip plan/tier/entitlement/feature booleans seen in the GET response of your own settings ; server often ignores Content-Type
techniques.tell: ⭐ THIS IS OUR PAYWALL ANSWER - paywalls have now ended 3 hunts (a paywalled SSRF lane, a paywalled AI feature, and a paid-tier-only product). Before declaring a feature 'paywalled and untestable', GET your own settings/entitlements object, find the boolean or tier string, and try to write it. Verify on STATE not response: reload the profile page and confirm the feature actually turned on. Revenue-impact framing (lost ad impressions / subscription devaluation) is what makes it pay.

techniques.technique: AUDIT THE READ SIBLING OF EVERY SECURED WRITE: the write handler derives identity from the SESSION (secure) while the matching read takes the same identity from the PATH (vulnerable). Nextcloud's setOutOfOffice used $userSession->getUser(), but GET /outOfOffice/{userId} and /{userId}/now never compared {userId} to the caller.
techniques.payload: for each POST/PUT that has no id in the path (implicitly 'me'), find the GET that DOES take {userId}/{id} and request another account's value ; also the /now, /current, /status, /summary variants of the same resource
techniques.tell: Asymmetry is the tell: if a write is 'me'-only but the read is parameterised, the read was probably added later by a different hand. Cheap and high-yield - a whole class our route-table sweep should flag automatically. Sensitive payloads hide in free-text fields (absence messages carried phone numbers and travel dates).

techniques.technique: DELETE THE COOKIE HEADER, DO NOT ONLY SWAP ACCOUNTS: our BOLA matrix tests A-vs-B, which misses endpoints that answer with NO session at all. A bug-tracker attachment endpoint /BugReport/Admin/Attachment/{id} returned file contents with the entire Cookie header removed.
techniques.payload: replay each object-fetch request three ways: (1) as victim's owner, (2) as attacker account, (3) with Cookie/Authorization header REMOVED ENTIRELY ; also try a bogus/expired token - some stacks fail open only on 'no header' and closed on 'bad header'
techniques.tell: Add the no-auth row to the auth matrix permanently - unauthenticated access is strictly more severe than cross-tenant and takes one extra request. Endpoints named /Admin/ that are reachable by normal users are the highest-value place to try it. Attachment/export/download/report routes are the usual offenders because they are served by a separate file handler that never saw the app's authz middleware.

techniques.technique: REPLAY THE AUTHORIZATION CODE, AND CHECK WHICH EXPIRY COLUMN IS READ: RFC 6749 4.1.2 requires single-use codes. Taskcluster's token handler never deleted the code row, and its expiry check read entry.client_details.expires (the requested CREDENTIAL lifetime, up to 1 year) instead of entry.expires (the code's own 10-minute life) - so a leaked code stayed replayable for months.
techniques.payload: POST /oauth/token with the same code twice -> two distinct access tokens = violation ; then wait past the documented code lifetime and exchange again ; repeat the same check on the token->credentials exchange leg
techniques.tell: Two independent bugs with one request each. Code leak paths that make it real: Referer on the redirect page, redirect-page logs, browser history, TLS-inspecting proxy. The wrong-column pattern generalises to any 'expires' check where the object embeds a nested config with its own expiry - read WHICH field the code compares, not whether an expiry exists at all. Also worth checking: does the code stay valid after the resulting token is revoked.

techniques.technique: SAVE THE DIRECT ASSET URL, DELETE THE OBJECT, THEN REFETCH AS SOMEONE ELSE: the app hides deleted items from its own listings while the underlying storage/DAV path keeps serving the bytes, and that path frequently has no per-request authz at all. On Nextcloud, /remote.php/dav/photos/{user_email}/albums/{album}/{photo} served another user's DELETED photo.
techniques.payload: capture the raw asset URL while the object exists -> delete it in the UI -> refetch (a) logged out, (b) as a different account ; note user-identifying path segments (email, username) that make the URL guessable for other tenants
techniques.tell: Two bugs in one flow: deletion is not real, AND the storage route skips authz. Pairs with [[strip-auth-entirely-not-just-swap-accounts]]. Watch for storage paths keyed by EMAIL - that makes cross-tenant enumeration trivial once you know a victim address. Always snapshot direct URLs (img src, download links, signed URLs) BEFORE any delete/trash/revoke test.

techniques.technique: RACE THE QUOTA CHECK: plan/tier limits (workspaces, folders, seats, free domains) are validated read-then-write with no lock, so N parallel creates all pass the check before any commits. Landed repeatedly: SingleStore workspaces (two separate reports), Dust folders, WordPress free-domain purchase.
techniques.payload: capture the CREATE request -> Burp Intruder 'send group in parallel' (or JS Promise.all of 15-30 fetches) ; vary one harmless unique field per request (name/meta) so dedupe does not merge them ; *** DELETE-THEN-BURST refinement (Dust): fill to the limit, delete ONE, then immediately burst - the freed slot plus the unlocked check lets many through
techniques.tell: Verify on STATE not response: reload the list and count objects > limit. Usually Low/Medium alone (resource abuse) but HIGH when the limit IS the paywall (seats/plan). Check scope first - many programs explicitly exclude DoS/resource-exhaustion; frame it as PLAN-LIMIT/REVENUE bypass, not DoS, and keep the burst small (10-20) so it never looks like a flood.

techniques.technique: PRE-INVITE PAST THE SEAT LIMIT (no race needed): the seat check runs at INVITE time only, never at ACCEPT time. Invite N users while under the cap; each can still sign up and join after the workspace is full, so a free tier carries unlimited members. Dust: 3-seat free plan -> 100 users.
techniques.payload: while under the limit, send invites to many addresses (email+alias) -> hit the cap so the UI says 'upgrade to add more' -> now register/accept as each pre-invited address and confirm each one lands INSIDE the workspace
techniques.tell: *** Directly applicable to any teammate / sub-account invite flow. The proof is the contradiction: the server tells the admin 'no seats remaining' while a pre-invited user joins fine. Revenue-loss framing is what makes it pay. Sibling checks at accept-time: expired invite still accepted, revoked invite still accepted, role re-read from the invite instead of the current plan.

techniques.technique: GRANT A PAID-TIER ROLE BY EDITING THE ROLE FIELD: the plan gate lives in the UI while the invite/share endpoint accepts any role value from a free account. Lovable: POST /projects/{id}/magic-codes with {access_level: read} produced a Pro-only 'Read access' invite link on a free plan, and the invited user really received that role.
techniques.payload: intercept the invite/share create call and swap the role/access_level/roleId/permission value to the premium-only one ; also try role ids harvested from docs or from a higher-tier account ; then ACCEPT the invite from the second account and confirm the effective role
techniques.tell: Pairs with [[paywalled-flag-flip-via-settings-api]] - that flips an entitlement on yourself, this grants a gated ROLE to someone else. Verify by accepting and reading the member list, never by the mutation response. Frame as subscription-control bypass (integrity + revenue), not IDOR.

techniques.technique: EMPTY/NULL THE SCOPE FIELD TO ESCAPE YOUR SCOPE: a sub-scoped admin (department/subuser/team/project) is confined by a scope id in the request. Sending that field EMPTY (or null, or omitted) makes the backend treat the action as global. Lark: a sub-department admin set department_id to an empty value and added users to the MAIN department.
techniques.payload: on every scoped write try scope='' | null | omit the key entirely | scope=0 | scope='*' | scope=parent-id ; compare all outcomes, they often differ
techniques.tell: *** First thing to try on sub-user / sub-account / teammate listings. Distinct from ordinary BOLA: you are not naming someone else's id, you are DELETING the constraint, so 'is this id mine?' checks never fire. Watch for a success whose result set is WIDER than before.

techniques.technique: DELEGATION THAT EXCEEDS THE DELEGATOR: B holds READ-ONLY plus re-share and can grant C WRITE. The re-share path validates that B may share at all, but never clamps the new grant to B's own permission set. (Nextcloud.)
techniques.payload: A grants B a LOW permission plus the ability to invite/share -> as B, share/invite C with a HIGHER permission (write/admin/owner) -> accept as C and exercise the higher right on A's object
techniques.tell: Applies to any nested grant: a member inviting with a bigger role, a subuser minting an API key with scopes it lacks, a teammate creating another teammate. The rule being broken is 'a grant must be a subset of the granter's rights'. Verify by having C perform the elevated ACTION, not by reading C's role label.

techniques.technique: REMOVE THE PARAMETER, DO NOT ONLY TAMPER IT: pricing/validation logic often branches on presence. LinkedIn premium checkout dropped to IDR 0.00 by DELETING serviceIdSwitchingFrom (and later optionalPriceIds) rather than editing any value - and the zero-price order actually completed ($2,500).
techniques.payload: for each field of a pricing/permission/verification request, resend with that field REMOVED (also null, empty string, empty array) - one at a time, then in pairs ; watch the computed total or granted permission in the response
techniques.tell: Different code path from value tampering: absent fields hit defaults and skip validators. The first variant became unreproducible after a partial fix but a second removal COMBO still worked - retest combinations before accepting 'fixed'. Same family: negative/oversized numbers passing client-only checks (negative file size, negative bid, quantity above max).

techniques.technique: THE VERIFICATION TOKEN IS IN YOUR OWN API RESPONSE: an endpoint listing your objects also serialises the pending-verification token for identifiers you do not own, letting you verify them yourself. Mozilla Monitor: /api/v1/user/breaches returned unverified emails WITH their verification tokens -> replay into /verify-email?token= and monitor any victim address.
techniques.payload: add a resource that needs email/phone/domain verification, then diff the FULL JSON of every list/detail endpoint for token|code|secret|nonce|verificationKey fields ; replay the found token into the public verify endpoint
techniques.tell: Read the raw response body, not the rendered UI - the front-end usually drops these fields. Same family: OTP or reset code echoed in a response, and OTP validators accepting placeholders such as 0000. Impact is unauthorised binding of someone else's identifier to your account.

techniques.technique: HOW TO ACTUALLY RUN A WEB RACE (the harness, not the theory): queue N requests but withhold the final byte of each, then release them together so they hit the server inside the same processing window. Turbo Intruder does this with the 'gate' argument; a browser with two tabs pre-filled and both submit buttons clicked together is the low-tech version that still won a Stripe bounty.
techniques.payload: Turbo Intruder: engine=RequestEngine(endpoint=target.endpoint, concurrentConnections=100, requestsPerConnection=100, pipeline=True) ; for i in range(30): engine.queue(target.req, gate='race1') ; engine.openGate('race1') ; engine.complete(timeout=60) . Plain JS equivalent: build N fetch() Promises then Promise.all() them. Plain curl: xargs -P N (weaker - no gate, but it beat a transactional-email product's limit check often enough to prove the point)
techniques.tell: The underlying defect is always CHECK-THEN-ACT on a re-resolved reference: the server reads the current count/state, decides, then writes - with no lock or unique constraint between. Same shape as the native TOCTOUs (curl stat-then-fopen, Rust remove_dir_all) but over HTTP. VERDICT ON STATE: reload the list and count objects, never trust the N success responses. ⚠️ Keep the burst small (10-30) and clean up: many programs exclude DoS/resource-exhaustion, so frame the finding as a LIMIT/INTEGRITY bypass and never as load.

techniques.technique: REPLAY A ONE-TIME TRANSACTION IN PARALLEL - the server credits it once per request instead of once per token. Reddit: replaying POST /api/v2/gold/android/verify_purchase with the SAME Google Play transaction_id 10x in parallel credited 9 of them (coins minted from one purchase). Stripe: a promotion code with redemption_limit=1 was redeemed twice by submitting two checkouts together.
techniques.payload: capture the settle/verify/redeem call, then fire the IDENTICAL body (same receipt id / coupon / voucher / referral code) N times in parallel ; targets: purchase-receipt verification (Google Play / App Store), coupon+promo redeem, gift-card top-up, referral or signup bonus, cashback, invite accept, 'claim free X'
techniques.tell: No token mutation needed - the same one-time identifier is the payload, which is what makes it trivially reproducible and easy to triage. Look for a missing unique constraint on (transaction_id) or a missing idempotency key. Direct financial impact, so this is usually the highest-paying race class. Check whether the balance actually moved before reporting - count the credited units, not the HTTP 200s.

techniques.technique: RACE THE SEAT / MEMBERSHIP JOIN: plan seat caps and join flows are read-then-write. Krisp /v2/seats raced past the maximum seat limit; HackerOne's own ctf.hacker101.com /group/join let one user join the SAME group 30x in parallel (duplicate membership rows corrupting group stats) - and that was a REGRESSION of an earlier fix.
techniques.payload: parallel-burst POST /seats | /members | /group/join?invite=<token> | /teammates | accept-invite ; also burst the SAME invite token from one account to create duplicate memberships
techniques.tell: Two distinct outcomes, report whichever appears: (a) member count exceeds the plan cap = revenue/plan bypass, (b) the SAME user appears multiple times = data-integrity corruption of stats/billing. Pairs with [[pending-invite-bypasses-seat-limit]] (the no-race variant) and [[parallel-burst-to-bypass-quota-and-delete-then-burst]]. ⚠️ Re-test known-fixed race bugs - the HackerOne one came back after an implementation change.

techniques.technique: PASSWORD RESET LEAVES OLD SESSIONS ALIVE: after an admin (or the user) resets a password, previously authenticated sessions keep working until natural expiry - so revoking access does not actually revoke it. Apache Airflow CVE-2023-40273: an attacker who had logged in kept full UI+API access after the admin reset that user's password, with no way to force logout short of rotating the secret key and restarting.
techniques.payload: log in as the victim in browser 1 -> change/reset the password from browser 2 (or as admin) -> refresh browser 1 and call an authenticated API ; also test after: email change, MFA enrolment, role downgrade, member removal, and API-key revocation
techniques.tell: The security claim being broken is 'reset the password to lock the attacker out' - frame it as incident-response failure, which is what makes it more than a session-hygiene nit. ⚠️ CHECK SCOPE FIRST: many programs explicitly non-qualify session management (some programs explicitly list 'no logout on password change' / 'session too long' as out of scope), so verify before spending time. Strongest variant is the ADMIN reset case - the admin is told the account is secured and it is not.

techniques.technique: Field the UI renders READ-ONLY (lock icon, no editor) is still accepted by the save endpoint. Send it in the normal profile/bio save body; no re-auth is required because the flow was never modelled as a credential change.
techniques.payload: POST /account/info/bio/v1  {"first_name":"x","last_name":"y","email":"attacker@evil.tld","role":"OWNER"}
techniques.tell: A field displayed with a padlock/greyed-out/'contact support to change' affordance, saved by the SAME endpoint as editable fields. Compare it to the sibling endpoint that DOES protect the same asset (e.g. /account/password requires old_password) - that asymmetry is the whole report.
techniques.source: Yelp for Business - locked email field silently editable via API
techniques.verify: Re-read the value on a DIFFERENT backend (GraphQL vs REST) to prove persistence rather than response echo. Then chain: forgot-password to the rewritten address -> real reset mail -> login. Email is the recovery anchor, so rebinding it is ATO, not a settings bug.

techniques.technique: A slider/dropdown whose MAXIMUM is computed server-side from your own history still accepts any value in the mutation. The bound lives only in the rendering code.
techniques.payload: {"operationName":"UpdateInvitationPreferencesMutation","variables":{"min_bounty":7000}}
techniques.tell: Any UI control whose limit is personalised ('based on your average payout', 'your plan allows up to N'). Personalised bound = computed for display = often not re-checked on write.
techniques.source: HackerOne - bypass minimum bounty amount in invitation preferences
techniques.verify: Re-query the object with the read query afterwards and confirm the out-of-range value persisted; a mutation returning was_successful:true is not proof.

techniques.technique: Send a scoping field EMPTY/null instead of changing its value. Empty often means 'no filter' to the backend rather than 'invalid'.
techniques.payload: {"department_id":""}   # instead of your own department id
techniques.tell: Any tenant/department/org/project scoping id present in a write body. Test null, "", 0, [] and omission separately - they take different code paths.
techniques.source: Lark Technologies - sub-dept user can add users to main department
techniques.verify: Confirm the created/moved object is readable by a user OUTSIDE your scope, with an own-scope control that still succeeds.

techniques.technique: Same logical field, two different endpoints, two different limits. Enumerate every route that writes a given field and take the weakest.
techniques.payload: registration form caps name at 32 chars; profile-update caps the same field at 50
techniques.tell: Multi-step signup vs later editing of the same object. Also API vs web vs mobile writers of one field.
techniques.source: Legal Robot - first/last name restriction bypass
techniques.verify: Write via the weak route, read via the strict one, and check the strict consumer renders/handles the over-length or out-of-range value.

techniques.technique: Client DECLARES a value the server then trusts as a limit (byte_size, content-length, duration, item count) when minting a presigned/signed artifact. Declare small, send large.
techniques.payload: POST /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads {'byte_size': 1} then PUT a 5GB body to the returned presigned URL
techniques.tell: Any 'get me an upload URL' handshake where the client states the size/type up front. Check whether the signed URL actually BINDS the header - AWS SDKs silently drop content-length from presigned URLs unless explicitly whitelisted.
techniques.source: Ruby on Rails - ActiveStorage direct upload fails to sign content-length
techniques.verify: Inspect the returned signed URL for the header in SignedHeaders; then upload an oversized body and confirm 200 rather than 403.

techniques.technique: A slot/index parameter documented as a small range (1..10) accepts arbitrary strings, turning a bounded resource into an unbounded one.
techniques.payload: imgnum=1  ->  imgnum=cow  /  imgnum=99999
techniques.tell: Parameters that look like an array index or slot number chosen by the UI, where the UI only ever emits values from a fixed list.
techniques.source: U.S. DoD - file upload restriction bypass via imgnum
techniques.verify: Fetch the object back at the arbitrary index; confirm it persists and does not overwrite the legitimate slots.

techniques.technique: Gate enforced only by a disabled button / client-side validator. Remove the disabled attribute or post the next step directly.
techniques.payload: remove disabled="disabled" and the is-disabled class, then submit; or POST the following step directly
techniques.tell: Terms acceptance, age gates, 'I have read', multi-step wizards where step N+1 has its own URL.
techniques.source: Acronis - no server side check on terms of service page
techniques.verify: Check the server-side record: does the account show terms_accepted=false while being fully usable? Impact is compliance/agreement integrity, not just a UI nit.

techniques.technique: Redemption-limited promo code consumed by TWO checkouts submitted simultaneously. Counter is read at payment start and written at completion, so both pass the check.
techniques.payload: open the same payment link twice, apply the code in both, click Pay in both within the processing window
techniques.tell: Any code/voucher with a 'redemption limit' or 'uses left' counter, where payment processing visibly takes seconds. NO tooling needed - two browser tabs is the PoC, which is exactly what stops it being downgraded as 'requires special tooling'.
techniques.source: Stripe - promotion code can be used more than redemption limit
techniques.verify: Read the discount object after: usage_limit unchanged and times_used still 1 while N transactions completed with the discount applied. ALSO run the sequential control - a later attempt must be REFUSED, proving the limit exists and only fails under concurrency.

techniques.technique: Replay an in-app-purchase receipt-verification call in parallel. The same store transaction_id/token is credited once per winning request.
techniques.payload: POST /api/v2/gold/android/verify_purchase  transaction_id=GPA...&token=...  x40 in parallel
techniques.tell: Receipt/entitlement verification endpoints (Google Play, App Store, Steam) that take a purchase token as input. The dedupe key exists but is checked non-atomically.
techniques.source: Reddit - race condition inflates coins at verify_purchase
techniques.verify: Check the credited balance, not the responses - 9 of 10 parallel requests succeeding is the finding. One purchase, N credits.

techniques.technique: Race the endpoint that consumes a quota (seats, subdomains, licences, members) to exceed a hard maximum.
techniques.payload: N parallel POST /v2/seats
techniques.tell: Any 'X of Y used' counter tied to a plan tier. Plan-limit bypass = paying for one tier and getting another, which is a revenue impact and frames better than 'rate limiting'.
techniques.source: Krisp /v2/seats seat limit; Chaturbate whitelabel subdomain limit
techniques.verify: Read the quota object afterwards: used > max. Keep the own-account control showing the limit is enforced sequentially.

techniques.technique: OAuth2 authorization code is never DELETED at token exchange, and the expiry check reads the wrong column (the requested credential lifetime instead of the code's own 10-minute expiry). Replay the code repeatedly.
techniques.payload: POST /login/oauth/token with the same code twice -> two distinct access tokens, both valid
techniques.tell: Single-use artifacts (auth codes, magic links, invites, reset tokens) where the handler VALIDATES but you cannot see a consume/delete. Also look for two different expiry fields on the same row - handlers pick the wrong one.
techniques.source: Mozilla Taskcluster - OAuth2 authorization codes reusable, wrong expiry column
techniques.verify: Exchange, then replay: a second 200 with a different token is the bug. Fix shape is an atomic DELETE ... WHERE code=? AND expires>now() RETURNING *.

techniques.technique: Time-limited override/grace period enforced against the LOCAL device clock. Move the clock to extend it indefinitely.
techniques.payload: admin issues a 10-minute override code; set device date forward/back to keep it alive
techniques.tell: Any countdown, trial, grace period or override whose remaining time could be computed client-side. Ask: is the deadline checked against server time on every use?
techniques.source: Cloudflare WARP - bypass admin override via local device time
techniques.verify: Confirm the privileged state persists past the intended window and that the server never re-validates.

techniques.technique: Race a CHANGE flow against its own CONFIRM flow. Request confirmation for an address you own, then change the pending value to the victim's and click the old confirmation link mid-write - the confirmation applies to the new value.
techniques.payload: 1) change email to mine, get link. 2) change email to victim@corp (intercept). 3) release, wait ~1s, visit MY link.
techniques.tell: Two endpoints touching the same row without a transaction: set-pending and confirm-pending. MEASURE the slow one first - the write took 1100-2500ms, which is what makes the window hittable by hand.
techniques.source: Shopify - bypass partner email confirmation to take over any store
techniques.verify: Check the account shows the victim address as CONFIRMED. Then exercise what confirmation unlocks (auto-join, collaborator conversion, store takeover) - the confirmed flag alone is not the impact.

techniques.technique: Race a join/claim endpoint to create DUPLICATE membership rows. The duplicate is not just a counting error - removal logic matches one row and leaves the other, producing an undeletable member.
techniques.payload: Turbo Intruder gate: 30 queued POST /group/post_join, then openGate
techniques.tell: Join/invite/claim/enrol endpoints where membership is a row rather than a unique constraint. Ask what DELETE does when two rows match.
techniques.source: HackerOne CTF - race condition in joining group / undeletable group member
techniques.verify: Verdict on the resulting STATE: try to remove the member as the admin and show it cannot be removed. Duplicate-state that breaks an admin action outranks a duplicate counter.

techniques.technique: Race a 'claim one of a limited pool' mutation to hold several pooled resources, denying them to other users.
techniques.payload: 22 parallel claimCredential mutations -> multiple distinct credential sets returned
techniques.tell: Anything worded 'claim', 'reserve', 'assign me a', 'check out' against a finite pool of test accounts, licences, coupons, IPs.
techniques.source: HackerOne - race condition in claiming program credentials
techniques.verify: Confirm you hold multiple DISTINCT items simultaneously; impact includes denial of the pool to legitimate users.

techniques.technique: A role with permission over area A can invoke a mutation that belongs to area B. Enumerate mutations from the bundle and fire them from the LOW-privileged session.
techniques.payload: {"query":"mutation{changeDomainEnforcementState(domainIds:[\"...\"],enforcementState:NOT_ENFORCED){...}}"}
techniques.tell: Org/admin consoles with fine-grained role checkboxes. Grant the low role exactly ONE unrelated permission, then aim it at every other mutation.
techniques.source: Shopify Plus - store management role can call changeDomainEnforcementState
techniques.verify: Own-object control from the high-privileged account plus the same call from the low role; the low role succeeding on a different area is the finding. NOTE: 'hidden page' access alone is non-qualifying on many programs - you must cross a real privilege boundary.

techniques.technique: A first-party app's own API returns the store/tenant ACCESS TOKEN in a response body the user can read. Removing the user later does not revoke it.
techniques.payload: open the embedded app, filter for its graphql call, read shopifyToken from the shopInfo response
techniques.tell: Embedded/first-party apps that talk to a DIFFERENT origin than the console. Grep every response for token/secret/key - and then test the token AFTER your access is revoked.
techniques.source: Shopify - unauthenticated access for removed staff via leaked Flow app token
techniques.verify: Use the token from a clean session with no cookies. Then have the admin remove your account and REPLAY - persistence after revocation is what turns a leak into a critical.

techniques.technique: Re-share escalation: a share received as READ-ONLY (but re-sharable) can be re-shared onward WITH WRITE.
techniques.payload: A shares read-only+resharable to B; B shares to C with write; C can edit
techniques.tell: Any delegation/re-share/sub-invite feature. Permissions on the derived grant are validated against the ACTOR's role, not clamped to the PARENT grant.
techniques.source: Nextcloud - re-sharing allows increase of privileges
techniques.verify: C actually writes and A sees the change. The invariant is: a derived grant can never exceed its parent.

techniques.technique: TOCTOU on an SSRF ALLOWLIST: the server resolves the hostname once to validate it and AGAIN to connect. Serve a 0-TTL DNS record that answers benign, then internal.
techniques.payload: delegate a subdomain to your own NS; return a public IP on query 1 and 169.254.169.254 on query 2
techniques.tell: Any user-supplied URL that is validated at save time and fetched later (webhook destinations, callback URLs, avatar import, proxy targets). If the validated IP is not PASSED to the connect call, the check is decorative.
techniques.source: Kubernetes - bypass apiserver proxy filter via TOCTOU DNS
techniques.verify: Prove two different answers were served to the two lookups. Works because most resolvers honour TTL 0 and Go/most runtimes have no local DNS cache.

techniques.technique: Consensus reflection: where peers exchange integrity attestations in no fixed order, observe a legitimate peer's submission and REPLAY it as your own.
techniques.payload: hook the receive handler, cache a peer's hash, submit the cached value when asked for yours
techniques.tell: Any protocol where all parties are expected to produce the SAME value and submission order is unconstrained. The fix shape (commit-reveal) tells you what the flaw was.
techniques.source: Nintendo Splatoon 3 - in-match integrity bypass via consensus reflection
techniques.verify: Confirm the tampered client is accepted by peers and in replay data. Generalises to any attestation/anticheat/quorum design.

techniques.technique: Buy a SECOND licence/plan alongside an existing one and watch which attributes survive the merge. Seat count took the NEW licence's value (4 users -> 1) while the expiry took the LONGER of the two (extended by 5 years). Buy the cheapest 5-year plan to extend an expensive short one.
techniques.payload: hold a 4-seat licence expiring soon; purchase a 1-seat 5-year licence; re-read the licence page
techniques.tell: Any product where two entitlements of the same type can coexist. The merge is usually written as 'take the max of the dates' without asking whether the entitlements are comparable. Ask: which field wins, and can I buy the cheap one to win it?
techniques.source: PortSwigger - incorrect logic when buying one more licence extends existing licence expiry
techniques.verify: Read the entitlement object before and after and diff EVERY field. The finding is a field that moved in the customer's favour without them paying for it.

techniques.technique: Enter a pending/'under review' state while entitled, then let the subscription EXPIRE. The review resolves later against a stale entitlement check and re-grants the badge/feature permanently.
techniques.payload: change profile photo 1 day before subscription expiry -> badge goes to review -> cancel subscription -> review completes -> badge returns for free
techniques.tell: Any asynchronous review, moderation or verification queue attached to a PAID feature. The grant happens when the reviewer clicks approve, and that code path rarely re-checks whether you are still a subscriber.
techniques.source: X / Twitter Blue - verified badge without purchase, subscription expiry not validated at review time
techniques.verify: Confirm the feature is still active after the paid period is provably over (store receipt / subscription page showing ended).

techniques.technique: Upgrade (or upgrade-then-downgrade) a plan immediately after an action that triggers review, to reset or skip the review state.
techniques.payload: change profile picture -> immediately upgrade to the higher tier -> review is skipped -> downgrade again
techniques.tell: Plan changes that rebuild the account/entitlement record. Any state attached to the OLD record (pending review, flags, strikes, quota used) may be dropped on rebuild. Test every plan transition against every pending state.
techniques.source: X / xAI - bypassing profile verification via premium plan upgrade
techniques.verify: Confirm the pending state is gone and the action took effect unreviewed.

techniques.technique: Currency arbitrage: prices are stored as a fixed table per currency and not re-derived from live FX. Pick the currency whose fixed price converts to the least.
techniques.payload: USD 399 vs EUR 349 while EUR/USD ~1.00 -> pay in EUR, save ~13%
techniques.tell: A price selector that offers several currencies with round numbers in each. Round numbers = hand-maintained table = drifts with the market. Compute today's cross-rate for every offered currency.
techniques.verify: Complete the purchase in the cheap currency and show the amount actually captured. Frame the impact as per-transaction leakage x volume, not as a pricing opinion.

techniques.technique: An 'accept this offer/credit' endpoint applies the grant EVERY time it is called. Replay it N times to stack N credits. Worth trying WITHOUT a race first - the naive call often just works.
techniques.payload: POST /ajax/accept_fee_discount_offer  id=fdo_...   x30  ->  30 x $20,000 of fee-free processing
techniques.tell: One-time account credits, fee waivers, promo grants, referral bonuses, goodwill credits - anything applied by clicking Accept in a dashboard banner. The offer id is the only input, so replay is trivial.
techniques.source: Stripe - fee discounts can be redeemed many times, unlimited fee-free transactions
techniques.verify: Read the credits/discounts API afterwards and count the applied grants. NOTE from this report: after the first fix a RACE still worked 23/30, so always re-test a fixed endpoint concurrently - 'already accepted' on some requests plus success on others is still the bug.

techniques.technique: Mine JS event handlers for PARAMETER NAMES the UI never sends, then send them yourself with the inverted value. A boolean discovered in an onClick handler flipped to false returned suspended/inactive records; OMITTING the key entirely gave a third behaviour.
techniques.payload: {"campaign_id":"0","product_name":"","page_index":1,"page_size":30,"live":false}
techniques.tell: Read the bundle for the handler that builds the request, not just the request. Then test THREE states per boolean: true, false, and absent - they take different branches and 'absent' is the one nobody tests.
techniques.source: TikTok Shop - exploitable live argument in onClick leads to data leakage of suspended products
techniques.verify: Compare returned record sets between the three states; the finding is records you cannot reach through any UI path.

techniques.technique: A numeric field the UI constrains with a widget (1-5 stars, 0-100%) accepts arbitrary magnitudes server-side.
techniques.payload: {"message":"x","rating":55}   # UI only ever sends 1..5
techniques.tell: Star ratings, percentages, scores, priorities, weights - anything the UI renders as a fixed set of choices. Bounds live in the widget, not the model.
techniques.source: inDrive - unlimited fake rate to passenger via /api/v1/reviews/ride/<id>/driver
techniques.verify: Read the aggregate afterwards (profile rating, leaderboard) and show the out-of-range value polluted it. Aggregate pollution is the impact, not the 200.

techniques.technique: Send a NEGATIVE size/quantity so a quota check passes by subtraction. The client recalculates and re-sends the size during upload, so the value is attacker-controlled at the moment it is checked.
techniques.payload: upload chunk with size = -1  ->  'not enough space' check passes
techniques.tell: Any client-declared size/count checked against a remaining balance. Negative is the cousin of huge - it is the one that slips past a 'value <= remaining' comparison.
techniques.source: LY Corporation - file sizes may be manipulated into negative numbers when uploading
techniques.verify: Confirm the upload completes despite the quota, and check whether the quota counter itself went UP (free storage).

techniques.technique: Feature hidden from the UI for your account state (unverified email, wrong plan) but the endpoint does not re-check. Perform the action on a fully-privileged account, capture the request, replay it with the restricted account's cookie.
techniques.payload: POST /voyager/api/publishing/contentSeries with an UNVERIFIED account's session
techniques.tell: 'You must verify your email to do X' / 'upgrade to unlock'. The gate is usually implemented as UI conditional rendering plus a check on the OBVIOUS endpoint, while sibling endpoints of the same feature are unguarded.
techniques.source: LinkedIn - unverified user can post newsletter which is not allowed through the UI
techniques.verify: Confirm the created object exists and is publicly visible, and that the restricted state is unchanged (still unverified). Capture-as-privileged / replay-as-restricted is the whole method.

techniques.technique: Try MAGIC OTP values before brute forcing: 0000, 1111, 1234, 000000, and the empty string. Some flows treat a placeholder as valid.
techniques.payload: {"phone":"<victim>","code":"0000"}  -> phone number rebound to the account
techniques.tell: Any 4-6 digit confirmation on a CHANGE flow (phone, email, payout account) rather than login. Change flows are written later and get less scrutiny than the login OTP.
techniques.source: inDrive - change phone number OTP flaw leads to phone number takeover
techniques.verify: Confirm the identifier is actually rebound by reading the profile, then chain to recovery - a rebound phone/email is the recovery anchor, so it is ATO not a settings bug.

techniques.technique: A CAPTCHA token is validated but never CONSUMED - solve once, replay the same CapAnswer/CapKey pair across unlimited submissions.
techniques.payload: reuse CapAnswer=U4YIQ & CapKey=... across N registration requests, varying only the email
techniques.tell: Registration/contact forms where the captcha answer and its key both travel in the body. If the key is not deleted server-side after the first success, it is a single-use token that is not single-use.
techniques.source: Tennessee Valley Authority - captcha bypass leads to register multiple users with one valid captcha
techniques.verify: N successes with one solved captcha. Frame as the downstream abuse the captcha existed to stop (mass account creation, mail flooding), not as 'no rate limit'.

techniques.technique: A security REQUIREMENT enforced on the primary path is not enforced on an alternate path into the same resource. 2FA was mandatory to submit to a program, but a collaborator INVITED to the report needed no 2FA to read it.
techniques.payload: account A (2FA on) files the report and invites account B (2FA off) as collaborator; B reads everything
techniques.tell: Any org-level policy - mandatory 2FA, SSO-only, IP allowlist, verified email. Enumerate EVERY way a principal can reach the protected resource: invite, share link, export, API token, mobile, support impersonation.
techniques.source: HackerOne - business logic error leads to bypass 2FA requirement via collaborator invite
techniques.verify: Show B holds the same data with the policy provably unmet. (This exact one was closed as a duplicate - the pattern is sound, the target was picked over.)

techniques.technique: Narrow an OTP brute force by reasoning about generation rather than trying the whole space. A 4-digit code was found in 8 attempts by only trying 6000-7000 after observing issued codes clustered there.
techniques.payload: POST /admin/login {'phone':'<admin>','code':'6xxx'} across 6000-6999, 20 threads, inside the 30s validity
techniques.tell: Short numeric codes with a short TTL and no attempt counter. Request several codes to YOUR OWN number first and look at their distribution before brute forcing anything.
techniques.source: inDrive - verification code brute force on truck-admin panel
techniques.verify: Log in and show authenticated content. Note admin phone numbers are often recoverable from WHOIS - recon feeds the auth attack.

techniques.technique: Revocation is honoured immediately but NOT durably - after ~20h the mobile client silently regained the revoked account via a background refresh. Test revocation on a DELAY, not just instantly.
techniques.payload: revoke 'Reddit on Android' at /account-activity, confirm the app breaks, then reopen the app the next day
techniques.tell: Any 'connected apps / active sessions / revoke access' screen. Revocation usually kills the access token but not the refresh token or a cached grant.
techniques.source: Reddit - app usable after revoking access; Shopify - disconnecting Google provider does not revoke session
techniques.verify: Wait 24h+ and confirm access returns with no re-authentication. Same family: disconnecting an OAuth provider or logging out not invalidating existing cookies.

techniques.technique: Export/CSV/PDF/print paths re-serialize objects WITHOUT the field-level redaction the UI applies. Fields marked internal-only, and objects in states the UI hides (drafts), appear in the export.
techniques.payload: GET /<program>/export_reports  ->  CSV contains DRAFT reports and 'Internal description' fields never shown in the web view
techniques.tell: Any Export / Download CSV / Print / Email digest button. Two separate reports on the same product both landed here. Ask: does the exporter reuse the same serializer as the view, or its own?
techniques.source: HackerOne - asset inventory internal descriptions leaked in CSV export; program managers can see draft reports via export
techniques.verify: Diff the export against what the UI renders for the same account - every extra column or extra row is the finding.

techniques.technique: Defeat a domain/username DENYLIST with a Unicode character that NORMALIZES to the blocked one after the check (Turkish dotted capital I).
techniques.payload: blocked: yopmail.com   accepted: yopmaİl.com  -> mail still delivers to yopmail.com
techniques.tell: Any allow/deny list applied to an email domain, username or hostname. The check runs on raw input; a later layer applies Unicode case-folding/NFKC. Reference table: 0xacb.com/normalization_table
techniques.source: Frontegg - bypassing security domain restriction with special characters
techniques.verify: Confirm the invite/registration actually reaches the blocked destination - delivery is the proof, acceptance by the form is not.

techniques.technique: Confused deputy via content reference: reference a PRIVATE object id inside a PUBLIC document, then bait a higher-privileged user into editing it. Their edit re-evaluates the reference under their permissions and silently widens the object's ACL.
techniques.payload: create a public task whose body contains {F27} (a private file id) plus obvious typos; wait for an admin to fix the typos
techniques.tell: Any markup that embeds objects by id ({F27}, urn:, gid://) where rendering permission is resolved per-viewer AND a save can persist a permission change. Look for 'the file will be made available' side effects on save.
techniques.source: Phabricator - user can link non-public file attachments, disclosed on edit by higher-privileged user
techniques.verify: After the privileged edit, fetch the object as the low-privileged user and confirm access. The victim never sees an indication.

techniques.technique: Moderation/report endpoints accept ids of UNPUBLISHED objects, and the moderation reply channel echoes their contents back to the reporter.
techniques.payload: POST /lite/flag-content?contentUrn=urn:li:jobPosting:<DRAFT id>&reason=SPAM_CONTENT
techniques.tell: Report/flag/appeal features. They are written to accept any content id and the automated 'we reviewed your report' notification quotes the content. Ask what OTHER channel returns data about an object you cannot read.
techniques.source: LinkedIn - attacker can flag draft job posts and disclose their details
techniques.verify: Confirm the notification contains fields of the unpublished object. The leak channel is the email/notification, not the HTTP response.

techniques.technique: Admin-side 'add member' path skips the acceptance step the invite flow requires, letting an admin place an arbitrary email into their org without consent.
techniques.payload: admin adds victim@corp by email; victim is a member without ever accepting
techniques.tell: Any two-sided consent (invite/accept, follow request, connection). Find the admin or bulk path and check whether it short-circuits the acceptance record.
techniques.source: Slack - bypass invite accept for victim
techniques.verify: Confirm membership from the victim's side with no acceptance event. Impact is phishing/trust-boundary, and org membership can carry SSO or data-sharing consequences.

techniques.technique: Staging/event storefronts left reachable with PLACEHOLDER prices ($0) and password protection toggled off between events.
techniques.payload: browse the event shop while the storefront password is disabled, add stock to cart, check out for $0
techniques.tell: Sub-brand shops on the vendor's own domain (book-bar., events., swag.). Password protection used as an on/off switch for an event is a schedule, not a control.
techniques.source: Shopify - exposure of employee summit page allows anonymous free orders
techniques.verify: Complete the order and confirm it reaches the merchant's order queue. NOTE: this exact report was closed INFORMATIVE because orders were manually verified before fulfilment - always check for a human step before claiming financial impact.

techniques.technique: WAF body-inspection SIZE LIMIT: inspection engines only read the first N bytes of a request body. Pad past the limit and the payload is never examined. AWS WAF inspects ~8KB, so 8192 filler bytes before the payload defeats it on POST.
techniques.payload: POST body: 'A'*8192 + <actual payload>
techniques.tell: Applies to EVERY injection class, not just XSS - if the WAF cannot see the body it cannot block SQLi, SSTI, command injection or SSRF either. Fingerprint the WAF first, then look up its documented inspection ceiling; every vendor has one and it is in their own docs.
techniques.source: Edr4/XSS-Bypass-Filters; kloudle.com AWS WAF 8KB body inspection limitation
techniques.verify: Send the same payload with and without the padding. Blocked -> allowed while the app behaviour is identical proves the bypass, not luck. Confirm the app actually parsed the padded body.

techniques.technique: Fingerprint the SANITIZER and its VERSION, then apply that version's known mXSS bypass, instead of spraying payloads. DOMPurify <2.1 and <2.0.1 both fall to namespace-confusion via math/mtext/table/mglyph/style, where the parser re-interprets the sanitized output.
techniques.tell: Client-side sanitizers ship their version in the bundle - grep the JS for DOMPurify.version / sanitize-html / xss / js-xss and read it. A pinned old version in package-lock or a vendored copy is the finding; the payload is then a lookup, not research.
techniques.verify: Confirm execution in the DOM, and record the exact library version from the bundle in the report - version + known-CVE mapping is what makes it undeniable rather than a filter-bypass opinion.

techniques.technique: Markdown renderers are a distinct XSS sink: the LINK TARGET is attacker-controlled and often not scheme-validated. Try javascript: and data: in link and image syntax, plus entity/whitespace-split variants.
techniques.payload: [a](javascript:alert(1))  |  [a](javascript://%0d%0aprompt(1))  |  ![a](data:text/html;base64,PHNjcmlwdD5hbGVydCgxKTwvc2NyaXB0Pg==)  |  ![a](x"onerror="alert(1))
techniques.tell: Anywhere users write formatted text: comments, issue/ticket bodies, product descriptions, profile bios, chat, PR reviews, wiki pages. The HTML sanitizer usually runs AFTER markdown->HTML, so it never sees the raw scheme; and image syntax lets you break out of the src attribute.
techniques.verify: Render it where OTHER users will see it - markdown fields are usually stored and shared, so this is stored XSS, not self-XSS. Confirm the anchor's href in the DOM, not just that the text appeared.

techniques.technique: Prefer NO-CLICK delivery: tags whose events fire on render or on state change, with no user interaction. Raises the finding from UI:R to UI:N.
techniques.payload: <details open ontoggle=[JS]>  |  <svg onload=[JS]>  |  <input autofocus onfocus=[JS]>  |  <marquee width=1 loop=1 onfinish=[JS]>  |  <svg><animate onbegin=[JS]>
techniques.tell: If your only working payload needs a click, keep going before filing - the same filter gap usually admits a self-firing tag, and several WAF-specific bypasses are published around <details/open/ontoggle>. Zero-click also removes the 'requires social engineering' objection triagers use to downgrade.
techniques.source: Edr4/XSS-Bypass-Filters - Without closing tag / Events / WAF sections
techniques.verify: Load the page in a clean session and touch nothing. Then state UI:N in the CVSS vector deliberately - it is a whole severity band.

techniques.technique: CROSS-ROOT ENDPOINT TRANSPLANT: harvest known paths from every subdomain of the organisation's OTHER root domains, then replay that path list against the in-scope target. Archive tools only know indexed hosts, so dev/staging/uat/regional assets return nothing - but they reuse the same framework and route table as their indexed siblings.
techniques.payload: gau across all subdomains of rootA.com, rootB.org -> strip to bare paths -> probe each against dev.target.tld with httpx
techniques.tell: Any programme with MANY assets, or an in-scope host that returns almost nothing from passive sources. Sibling roots are found from the programme scope itself, WHOIS/ASN, favicon hash and TLS SAN entries. The paths are free - you are transplanting, not guessing.
techniques.verify: Probe with status + title + content-length and diff against the target's 404 body; a soft-404 template makes 200s meaningless. Only in-scope hosts.

techniques.technique: PIN THE EXACT PRODUCT VERSION PRE-AUTH by hashing theme-independent STATIC ASSETS against a per-release database, bounding the range by which files exist at all, and intersecting with a behavioural floor (which protocol features the endpoint supports). Works even when the version string is masked.
techniques.payload: hash /common/<product>/**.css|.js -> match per-release table; file present/absent -> bounds; OIDC discovery fields (e.g. RFC 9207 iss param, DPoP) -> minimum version
techniques.tell: Off-the-shelf components in scope - SSO/IdP (Keycloak), CMS (TYPO3, PrestaShop, WordPress), admin panels. Version + public advisory beats hunting a custom bug, and the ASSET-HASH method survives a masked version banner where a header or /version endpoint does not.
techniques.verify: Report the exact version and how it was determined (which asset hashes, which behavioural floor) - that is what turns 'possibly vulnerable' into a defensible finding. Then confirm the advisory's actual precondition, do not assume version implies exploitable.

techniques.technique: MAKE IDENTITY STRUCTURAL, NOT A DISCIPLINE: one isolated browser profile per test identity (separate cookie jar/storage), a colour bar injected into every page, and a per-identity header stamped by an upstream proxy so the intercepting proxy's history shows WHICH account sent each request.
techniques.payload: profile-per-user browser configs -> mitmdump instance per profile injecting X-<Tag>-Color -> single Burp listener
techniques.tell: Every multi-account test (BOLA, BFLA, cross-tenant, invite flows) depends on knowing which identity fired a request. Doing that by remembering which tab you are in is how a self-access gets written up as cross-tenant access - the failure is silent and every status code still looks right.
techniques.verify: Before trusting any multi-identity result, confirm the marker in the proxy history matches the identity you believe you used. This replaces the manual identity-guard step rather than adding to it.

techniques.technique: Before mining JS bundles for a route table, check the docs site for /llms.txt — the 'index for AI agents' convention. It lists EVERY documented page and API operation, and on ReadMe-hosted docs each page has a .md twin (<host>/reference/<slug>.md) that carries the RAW OpenAPI definition: exact path, method, path/query params and request-body schema.
techniques.payload: curl -s https://<docs-host>/llms.txt  then  curl -s https://<docs-host>/reference/<slug>.md
techniques.tell: Server-rendered apps (Rails/Django/Laravel) have no SPA bundle to mine, so bundle-mining returns nothing and it is easy to conclude there is no route table. Vendors publishing a public API almost always ship docs, and the docs ARE the route table - deliberately served, zero traffic on the target app, no scanner, no ToS risk. Look for a hidden 'For AI agents: visit /llms.txt' div on the docs home. Also read robots.txt on the app itself: Disallow entries name real path families.
techniques.verify: Diff the documented operations against what the UI actually calls. The gap - operations no UI touches, especially ones taking a caller-supplied tenant/merchant id in the PATH - is the attack surface. Confirm each still exists before building on it; docs drift.

techniques.technique: Next.js SERVER ACTIONS are an invisible endpoint class: they never appear in a HAR as a named route and are absent from any OpenAPI/route list, yet they are server-side mutations reachable by anyone. Recover them from the client bundle and call them directly.
techniques.payload:
grep -ho 'createServerReference("[0-9a-f]\{40\}",[^)]*' *.js   # -> id + the ACTION NAME as the last string arg
POST /<any-app-route>
  Next-Action: <40-hex id>
  Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8
  body: ["arg1","arg2"]   # positional JSON array
techniques.tell: Bundle contains createServerReference("<40 hex>", callServer, void 0, findSourceMapURL, "<actionName>"). The name tells you what it does (switchAccount, clearSession, redirectToExternal). Actions that take a TENANT/ACCOUNT/ORG id are the prize.
techniques.verify: Response is an RSC stream and is often IDENTICAL for valid, cross-tenant and garbage input (all 303) — the action's response proves nothing. Verdict on STATE: run the action, then read a tenant-scoped endpoint and check WHOSE data comes back, with an own-object control in the same batch.

techniques.technique: Mine bundles PER HOST and AFTER login. An unauthenticated page ships only the auth chunks, and a multi-host app (Rails admin + Next.js dashboard) has a different bundle set per host. 'It is server-rendered, there is nothing to mine' is a false conclusion drawn from one host, logged out.
techniques.payload: login -> capture session cookie -> curl -L each authed route -> extract "/_next/static/...js" (or /packs/js/...) from EVERY page -> dedupe -> fetch -> extract paths
techniques.tell: Pre-login chunk count is small (27 chunks -> 10 paths). Post-login it jumps (35 chunks -> 24 paths, 8 never seen). Also check whether the auth cookie's Domain is the PARENT domain — if so ONE token authenticates every host in the flow, including the one you thought needed separate creds.
techniques.verify: Diff the post-login path set against the HAR and against any published API list; the gap is the target.

techniques.technique: Password-reset host poisoning: the HTTP status NEVER decides it. X-Forwarded-Host / X-Host / X-Forwarded-Server are commonly accepted at the HTTP layer (302, request queued) while the mailer still builds the link from a configured host. Only the EMAIL BODY is the verdict.
techniques.payload: POST /password  user[email]=<own>  -H 'X-Forwarded-Host: <attacker>'   then READ THE INBOX and check the link's host
techniques.tell: An absolute 'Host:' override usually 422s at the edge/CDN, which tempts you to declare the class tested. It is not — the forwarded-header variants are the real test, and they answer 302 either way.
techniques.verify: Send ONE poisoned reset in isolation, then read the NEWEST mail. Most frameworks (Devise) keep only the newest token, so an older link behaves EXACTLY like garbage — a stale token makes the whole test void, never 'enforced'.

techniques.technique: Aim mass assignment at the UNAUTHENTICATED endpoints that still WRITE the user record — password reset, email verification, signup completion, invite acceptance. They update a privileged row with no session, so a permitted-params slip there is a direct privilege grant.
techniques.payload: PUT /password  user[reset_password_token]=<tok>&user[password]=<new>&user[password_confirmation]=<new>&user[role]=admin&user[account_role]=admin&user[admin]=true&user[super_admin]=true
techniques.tell: Any pre-auth flow whose form posts a user[...] hash. The visible fields are 2-3; the model has dozens.
techniques.verify: Re-read the identity endpoint (/me) after the write and compare the role field to its PRE-TEST baseline — a role that was already 'admin' of its own tenant looks like success and is not. Confirm the write landed at all (login with the new password / check last_password_change_at) or a no-op reads as 'enforced'.

techniques.technique: PER-OPERATION PERMISSION, NOT PER-SCREEN. The UI hides an admin screen from a low role, but the underlying operation (REST route or GraphQL mutation) never checks which permission it requires. Log in as the LOW role, then call the operations that role's UI never renders. This is the field-level lesson of our own #941 promoted to the OPERATION level: the UI exposes a subset, the API accepts the whole set.
techniques.payload: as low-role user: enumerate operations from the published OpenAPI/GraphQL schema, diff against what the low-role UI actually renders, then invoke the missing ones directly with that role's own token/session
techniques.tell: A product with granular permission names (Store Management vs User Management, Reader vs Writer vs Admin) and a large operation count. The more operations, the worse the odds every one re-checks. Published OpenAPI or introspection makes the diff free.
techniques.verify: Own-object control first: the SAME call as the HIGH role must succeed, so a failure is authz and not a malformed request. Verdict on STATE - re-read the object as the high role and confirm the change actually landed; a 200 from a turbo-stream or generic handler proves nothing.
techniques.source: Shopify disclosed report - Store Management permission could call changeDomainEnforcementState

techniques.technique: DELEGATION MUST INTERSECT, NEVER EXCEED. Where a user can re-share, re-delegate or invite onward, check whether the second grant can be WIDER than the first. Classic shape: A grants B read-only but with re-share rights; B then shares to C and adds WRITE. The re-share path never intersects the new permission set with the original one.
techniques.payload: A -> B: read-only + may-reshare. B -> C: read+write. Then act as C and attempt the write A never authorised.
techniques.tell: Any re-share, sub-team, nested group, service-account, or invite-onward feature. Same family as token capability intersection but at the SHARING layer, where it is far less often tested.
techniques.verify: Three identities are required, and the control is A's own grant: confirm A really is read-only first. Verdict on state - C must actually modify the object, not merely receive a 200 on a share record.
techniques.source: Nextcloud disclosed report - re-sharing allows increase of privileges

techniques.technique: REVOCATION MUST KILL ALREADY-GRANTED ACCESS PATHS. Removing a user, downgrading a role or deleting a membership usually updates the permission table - but leaves previously issued artefacts alive: direct object/CDN URLs, signed links, cached responses, existing sessions, and API tokens minted while the role was higher.
techniques.payload: as the low role, capture a direct artefact/CDN URL and mint an API token; have the owner REMOVE the member or downgrade the role; then replay both the URL and the token
techniques.tell: Artefacts served from a different host than the app (CDN, object storage, static domain) are the usual miss, because the permission check lives in the app and the URL does not go through it. Also: tokens minted at a higher role and never re-evaluated after downgrade.
techniques.verify: Capture BEFORE revoking, replay AFTER. Control = a second URL/token that should still work (own object, untouched membership), so a failure is revocation and not an expired link.
techniques.source: GitLab disclosed report - removed guest still read job artefacts via the CDN URL

techniques.technique: IDENTITY FROM THE BODY INSTEAD OF THE SESSION on profile/settings UPDATE endpoints. The read path is scoped to the session, so the object looks safe, but the WRITE path takes id/email/userId out of the request body and updates whatever it names.
techniques.payload: POST /updateUser with the victim id and email substituted for your own, everything else unchanged
techniques.tell: An update endpoint whose body echoes an identifier the UI never lets you edit. If the id is present in the body at all, the server had a chance to trust it.
techniques.verify: Two accounts. Verdict on the VICTIM object: log in as the victim and confirm the field changed. Control = the same request with your own id must succeed.
techniques.source: MTN Group disclosed report - /app/updateUser had no authorisation check on the target id

techniques.technique: FastAPI (and most Python API frameworks) mount an INTERACTIVE SCHEMA at default paths that are frequently left unauthenticated in production. Hitting them hands you the complete route table, request bodies and auth requirements for free - the same win as a published OpenAPI, but on apps that never intended to publish one.
techniques.payload: /docs   /redoc   /openapi.json   /api/docs   /api/v1/docs   /api/openapi.json   /swagger   /swagger-ui
techniques.tell: The framework fingerprint is the trigger: a 422 whose body is {'detail':[{'type':...,'loc':['body','field'],'msg':'Field required'}]} is Pydantic, i.e. FastAPI. Also uvicorn in errors or Server headers. Check the schema paths on EVERY host of the app, not just the main one - internal or secondary subdomains are where it survives.
techniques.verify: Compare the schema against what the UI actually calls. The operations present in the schema but absent from the UI are the target set - especially anything under an auth or admin prefix.
techniques.source: Disclosed writeup - /docs exposed on a FastAPI subdomain led to an unauthenticated reset-password route

techniques.technique: AUTH-ROUTE SIBLING SWEEP. When one route in the auth family is missing its check, the siblings usually are too - they are written together and reviewed together. Having found reset-password unauthenticated, immediately test change-password, verify-email, confirm, set-password, resend, and any MFA enrol/disable route with the SAME shape. Two weak siblings chain into a full takeover that neither gives alone.
techniques.payload:
POST /auth/reset-password {username}            -> resets to a known default and RETURNS it
POST /auth/change-password {username, old_password, new_password}  -> no session required
POST /auth/login {username, new_password}        -> takeover, and the real owner is locked out
techniques.tell: Reset/change endpoints whose body carries the IDENTITY (username, email, userId) rather than a token. If the identity is in the body, the server had the chance to trust it. A response that states the new credential in plain text is the strongest possible confirmation.
techniques.verify: Two invariants, test both: (1) a reset must require proof of mailbox control - a token - not just a username; (2) a reset must NEVER disclose the resulting credential in the response. Use only accounts you own on BOTH sides; resetting a real user's password locks them out and is destructive.
techniques.source: Disclosed writeup - unauthenticated reset-password + change-password chained to account takeover

techniques.technique: REPLAY THE COMMIT STEP, NOT THE ENTRY STEP. A privileged multi-step action checks authorisation when the FORM loads, then assumes the confirm/commit request can only be reached legitimately - so the final request carries no check of its own. Perform the action as the HIGH role, capture the final request, replay it with the LOW role's session or token.
techniques.payload:
as admin: load admin form (step 1, ACL enforced) -> submit confirm (step 2)
capture step 2, swap in the low-privilege session/token, replay verbatim
e.g. POST /admin-roles  username=SELF&action=upgrade&confirmed=true
techniques.tell: Any action that spans two requests: load-then-confirm, request-then-apply, draft-then-publish, review-then-approve. The wider the gap between the gating screen and the committing call, the likelier only the screen is guarded.
techniques.verify: Control both ways: the SAME captured request must succeed with the high-role credential (proves the request is well formed) and the low-role credential must be able to do the entry step legitimately (proves the session is live). Verdict on state - re-read the object as the high role and confirm the change landed.
techniques.source: PortSwigger access-control KB, multi-step and context-dependent enforcement

techniques.technique: WORKFLOW STATE FLAWS - skip, drop, strip, or re-context. Steps linked by redirects and client-supplied params rather than server-side state can be (a) SKIPPED by replaying a later step directly, (b) DROPPED by discarding a request the client was supposed to make, (c) STRIPPED by removing a parameter that carries the check, or (d) RE-CONTEXTED by changing an attribute AFTER validation passed.
techniques.payload:
skip:      replay the confirmation/success request without completing the paid or approved step
drop:      intercept and DISCARD the role-selector / consent / step request, then continue - the state may default open
strip:     remove the parameter that carries the check entirely (e.g. current-password on a change-password call)
re-context: register with an ordinary value, pass validation, then CHANGE it to the privileged one
techniques.tell: Multi-step flows whose progress is carried in GET params, redirects or hidden fields instead of a server-side session flag. Removing a parameter is the most under-tested of the four - most testers change values, few delete the key.
